articles.title: Ukraine: Zelensky says war looks set to go on winter
articles.body:
Ukraine: Zelenskyy says war looks set to go on into winter
Published September 7, 2026last updated September 7, 2026
What you need to know
- Ukraine's president says the war with Russia appears likely to continue into winter
- His comments came after talks with visiting US envoys produced no announced breakthrough
- Russian officials say Ukrainian drone attacks killed two people in separate strikes in the Perm and Belgorod regions
Here are the latest developments in Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, September 7:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
UN rights chief urges ban on fully autonomous weapons
The UN human rights chief has called for an urgent ban on weapons that can kill without human involvement, citing reports that fully autonomous drones have already caused deaths in Ukraine.
Volker Türk said he was "horrified" by reports that Russian forces used a fully autonomous drone to kill three Ukrainians last month, while also noting reports that Ukraine had field-tested similar systems.
The New York Times reported last month that a Russian drone guided entirely by artificial intelligence killed three civilians in Zaporizhzhia in southeastern Ukraine on July 6.
According to the report, human operators had programmed the drone to travel toward a particular petrol station, but the system itself selected the precise target, thought to have been propane tanks.
Türk, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, also highlighted reports that Ukraine had tested autonomous weapons.
There has been growing pressure from international organizations and NGOs to regulate so-called lethal autonomous weapons, sometimes referred to as "killer robots."
"I join calls for the urgent prohibition of weapons that can take lives without human involvement," Türk told the UN Human Rights Council.
After years of debate, 128 countries agreed at the UN on Saturday on a definition of autonomous weapons.
NGOs have accused the United States and Russia in particular of trying to weaken the agreed language.
Zelenskyy says Russian drone targeted SBU chief's office
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that a Russian drone which struck the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in Kyiv on Friday had been aimed directly at the office of the agency's chief.
The revelation adds to the significance of one of the most high-profile Russian strikes on a Ukrainian government building since the start of the full-scale invasion.
SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad was not there at the time and was unharmed.
Zelenskyy said he had instructed the SBU to prepare an "appropriate, tangible response" and suggested Ukraine could retaliate in a similar manner.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike a "major escalation."
Black smoke was seen rising from the SBU building, close to the UNESCO-listed St. Sophia Cathedral.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least 12 people were wounded in the wider attack on the capital, although it was not immediately clear whether any of them were injured at the SBU headquarters.
The strike also damaged nearby buildings and shattered windows in the area.
It was the first time the SBU headquarters had been hit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
The SBU plays a central role in Ukraine's war effort and has carried out long-range and covert operations against Russian military targets. It was behind Operation Spiderweb in 2025, when drones targeted Russian strategic bombers at air bases deep inside Russia, as well as the 2022 bombing of the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.
Russia, North Korea open first road bridge
Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River, expanding transport links as political, economic and military ties between Moscow and Pyongyang deepen.
Read more about the story here.
Ukrainian drone attacks kill 2 in Russia, officials say
Attacks with drones killed at least two people and injured several others in Russia, regional authorities have said.
One person was killed and four others were injured in Russia's Perm region after a drone attack damaged a residential building, regional Governor Dmitry Makhonin said.
He said local air defense units had shot down 27 Ukranian drones over the region, which lies deep inside Russia.
In the Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, one person was killed and another injured in a separate Ukrainian drone attack, according to local authorities.
Reuters said it could not independently verify the reports. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.
No end in sight after diplomatic effort, says Zelenskyy
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the war with Russia currently appears likely to continue into the winter, after talks with visiting US envoys in Kyiv.
The talks produced upbeat assessments from both sides but no announced breakthrough in efforts to end the war.
"We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter — and this is how it appears at the moment," Zelenskyy said.
He also said Ukraine would hold talks with the US, France and Germany, without giving further details.
Zelenskyy again argued that the most difficult territorial issues could only be resolved in a meeting between leaders.
US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, had traveled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
Putin had announced a three-day pause in attacks on Kyiv for the duration of the US negotiators' visit. Ukraine, in turn, refrained from attacking Moscow during the same period.
Zelenskyy joked that the presence of Witkoff and Kushner had "worked better than the Patriot air defense systems."
It was Witkoff and Kushner’s first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a repeated target of Russian strikes since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion. The pair have made several visits to Moscow.
While Witkoff and Zelenskyy both described Sunday's talks positively, neither side announced a concrete breakthrough.
Welcome to our coverage
You join us after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy downplayed hopes of a quick end to the conflict, saying the fighting currently appears likely to continue into winter.
He was speaking after talks in Kyiv with US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.
Meanwhile, Russian officials say Ukrainian drone attacks have killed at least two people and injured several others.
Stay with us here for these stories and more from Russia's war in Ukraine.

articles.title: India to arm Su-30MKI fighters with hypersonic Russian air-to-air missile – report
articles.body:
India to arm Su-30MKI fighters with hypersonic Russian air-to-air missile – report
India is reportedly working on a plan to equip the Indian Air Force’s workhorse Sukhoi-30MKI fighter jets with advanced long-range Russian air-to-air missiles.
The Indian Defense Ministry is expected to consider a proposal to modify the Su-30MKI fleet to carry the Russian RVV BD air-to-air missiles, which can fly at hypersonic speeds and take out targets up to 300 kilometers away, ANI news agency reported.
The RVV BD is the export version of the R-37M missile, one of the world’s longest-range air-to-air missiles. It is designed to shoot down tanker and early warning aircraft past enemy fighter escort from long range. The Defense Acquisition Council meeting on Monday is expected to take up the proposal, the report said, citing sources.
The RVV BD is compatible with Russia’s advanced fifth-generation Su-57 fighter jet – which has already been offered to India.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is set to visit New Delhi later this week for the 18th summit of BRICS nations. A discussion on the possible sale of the Su-57 was on the agenda of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation held last month in Moscow.
New Delhi, which exchanged missile and drone strikes with nuclear-armed neighbor Pakistan last year, is rapidly modernizing its Sukhoi-30s. The planes have been modified to carry the air-launched version of the Brahmos supersonic cruise missile, and their avionics and electronic warfare suites are being upgraded under the ‘Super Sukhoi’ program.
The upgrades have taken on a new urgency as China has moved its J-20 fifth-generation aircraft next to the Indian border in Tibet, and is reportedly planning to transfer its J-35 fifth-generation fighters to Pakistan.
A defense acquisitions panel on Monday, chaired by Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, cleared a slew of proposals worth $11.64 billion to enhance the “war-fighting capability” of the air force, and various systems for the navy and the army.
”This upgrade is going to be formidable,” retired Air Marshal Anil Chopra told RT India.
He said India has been diversifying its defense purchases, but also maintaining strategic autonomy, despite US sanctions.
”Threats are being given to us for purchasing Russian oil and also weapon systems. We’re continuing to upgrade and use the Russian system,” he said. “Ours is a time-tested relationship.”
The Indian Air Force operates about 258 Su-30MKI – an India-specific variant of the multi-role fighter aircraft – and state-owned Hindustan Aeronautics Limited is producing 12 more at its Nashik facility to replace those lost in accidents over the years.
The jets saw action during last year’s clash with Pakistan – which India code-named Operation Sindoor – covering Indian formations and firing Brahmos missiles at Pakistani airbases.

articles.title: Iran’s retaliatory fire sends US warships fleeing, exposes American vulnerability

Iran’s retaliatory fire sends US warships fleeing, exposes American vulnerability

In a dramatic assertion of regional naval control, the IRGC’s Aerospace Force launched multiple ballistic missiles targeting a primary US aircraft carrier and an American destroyer participating in Washington’s illegal naval blockade against the Islamic Republic, forcing the vessels to withdraw.
The force staged the reprisal against the vessels “belonging to the child-killing, aggressor US military that had been harassing Iranian vessels and participating in the blockade,” the Corps said in an official statement released on Saturday.
“After sustaining damage and fearing another reprisal, the two warships were forced to flee the area of engagement,” the statement added.

Referring directly to the admission, the IRGC noted how the “aggressor enemy, which for years had swaggered around the region with false pride and hollow claims, was today forced to officially acknowledge that two US Navy warships had come under strikes.”
The IRGC emphasized that CENTCOM’s official acknowledgment of the strike serves as living evidence of the enemy’s strategic defeat and proof of the IRGC’s formidable offensive capabilities.
The IRGC asserted that the Corps, alongside the rest of Iran’s Armed Forces, remains fully committed to defending the Islamic Republic’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national security.

Victory belongs to the resilient people of Islamic Iran, while defeat and regret are the inevitable fate of the aggressors.”
The Corps expressed firm confidence that the bravery displayed by the Armed Forces—bolstered by nationwide popular support for defensive and retaliatory operations—would consistently prevent the enemy from achieving its sinister objectives.
Earlier, the IRGC unveiled previously unreleased operational footage documenting its decisive actions against non-compliant foreign vessels in the vital Strait of Hormuz. The released imagery debunked Washington’s claims of effectively escorting and supporting trespassing vessels through the maritime choke-point.
“The United States is the greatest threat to the security of regional countries and maritime trade; US support and escort operations are nothing but a big lie!” the IRGC cautioned. Demonstrating total operational awareness along its maritime boundaries, the IRGC Navy targeted and neutralized a Remotely Operated Vessel (ROV) belonging to the US military off Iran’s southern coast.

“With the grace and favor of Almighty God, every desperate move by the enemy is being closely monitored by brave, self-sacrificing IRGC Navy forces and will be met with a decisive attack,” the statement noted.
Reiterating national control over key sea lanes, the IRGC emphasized that the Strait of Hormuz “is under the management of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and that any move by the child-killing enemy will receive a firm response. The aggressor United States must understand that it has no choice but to leave the region and stop its acts of mischief.”
Simultaneously, the Aerospace Force of the IRGC extended its anti-reconnaissance umbrella to neutralize airborne spying apparatuses operating in neighboring airspace. Iranian defense forces shot down a 35-meter-long US military surveillance balloon over Erbil in northern Iraq. The targeted airborne platform was capable of carrying up to 500 kilograms of payload and operated at an altitude of approximately 750 meters. Tasnim news agency reported on Sunday that the strike forms part of a systematic strategy aimed at dismantling Washington’s regional reconnaissance and early-warning networks.
The retaliatory strikes by Iranian armed forces come against a background of severe, unlawful military aggression by American forces on Iranian territory and civilian centers.
Larak Island attack: On Monday, US armed forces launched a direct military assault on Iran’s Larak Island, located strategically in the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in the martyrdom of several individuals.
Strikes across Khuzestan: US missile strikes struck three distinct locations near Ahvaz and Aghajari in Khuzestan Province on Tuesday, martyring seven people and wounding eight others, according to provincial officials.
Kuhestak Wedding Ceremony Bombing: US forces struck a residential building in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province on Tuesday, while a local wedding reception was taking place. The strike resulted in the martyrdom of at least five people and wounded 68 others, including women and children.
In direct response to these violations, Iran’s armed forces executed coordinated salvos of retaliatory missile and drone strikes targeting hostile US military positions and bases spread across Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain. Furthermore, Iranian defensive actions led to the striking of three additional US-linked vessels that attempted to breach Iranian security zones or facilitate hostilities.
The current combat operations mark an intensification of the conflict that erupted on February 28, when the United States and Israel initiated unprovoked, large-scale military attacks against Iran in clear violation of the United Nations Charter.
Since February 28, Washington has repeatedly violated international law, targeting sovereign territory, critical national infrastructure, and civilian neighborhoods. However, Tehran's defense strategy has transformed the confrontation into an operational strain on the US military.
Independent security analysts and strategic defense reports confirm that the continuous deployment of interceptors against complex Iranian missile and drone salvos has severely depleted US military stockpiles.
Interceptor exhaustion: US stocks of key interceptors, including Patriot PAC-3 and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missile systems, have been depleted by well over half.
Strategic vulnerability: Defense intelligence estimates indicate that the rapid consumption of these high-cost interceptor inventories has pushed American air defenses in multiple theaters to critical levels, creating global operational gaps that will take defense manufacturers years to rebuild.
While Washington faces a rapidly shrinking stockpile of high-grade munitions and logistical strain, Iran’s defense doctrine—built upon domestic production, underground missile facilities, and vast stockpiles of asymmetric assets—has demonstrated enduring strength.
Despite sustained military pressure and illegal blockades from Washington, the national resilience of the Islamic Republic remains unbroken. The defensive actions executed by the IRGC have consolidated popular support across Iran, proving that threats and military coercion cannot alter Tehran's posture.
By striking high-value naval assets, enforcing strict control over the Strait of Hormuz, dismantling American intelligence platforms, and enduring external attacks, Iran's armed forces continue to demonstrate that foreign aggression will consistently carry unacceptable costs. As the IRGC leadership affirmed, the Iranian nation stands stronger than ever, fully prepared to maintain its sovereignty and deliver decisive responses to any future hostile miscalculations.

articles.title: Kim Jong-un vows nuclear-armed navy as North Korea expands military ambitions
articles.body:
North Korea’s Leader Kim Jong Un has vowed to build North Korea's navy into a nuclear-armed force, state media reported as US allies' maritime drills kicked off.
This week's manoeuvres involving Japan, South Korea and the United States were established in 2023 in what officials called an effort to deter Pyongyang's missile and nuclear threats.
Kim's comments came at the commissioning of the Kang Kon, a warship that partially capsized when launched in May 2025, in the port city of Wonsan on Sunday, the official Korean Central News Agency reported.
"We should make sure that the diversified and effective operation of nuclear combat systems is conducted for an actual war through developing our navy into a nuclear-armed force," Kim reportedly told the ceremony on Monday.
"Once ordered anytime, the new-generation destroyer should deal a deadly retaliatory blow at the enemies as it is a force involved in the state nuclear counteraction system," he said.
Photos released of Kim showed him accompanied by his daughter, Ju Ae, who is reportedly designated as his successor.
In July, Kim oversaw a test of the Kang Kon, one of two 5,000-tonne-class warships launched last year, just over a year after it was damaged during launch.
Kim's reference to a "nuclear-armed navy" suggests the vessels could serve as launch platforms for tactical nuclear-capable cruise missiles, said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University.
“Directly and within range"
Kim also said North Korea was carrying out an "important plan" to strengthen its navy that would be demonstrated to the world "in eight months".
That could foreshadow the unveiling of a major strategic asset, such as a new submarine capable of carrying submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs), Lim said.
By deploying the Kang Kon in the East Sea, Pyongyang is also seeking to keep the joint maritime exercises and deployments of nuclear assets "directly and within range", Lim said.
This week's US allies' drills, dubbed Freedom Edge, are set to run to Friday in international waters east and south of South Korea's Jeju Island.
The manoeuvres have pushed ahead despite President Donald Trump curtailing another set of drills with South Korea as the US leader aims to reopen diplomacy with Pyongyang about its nuclear programme.
North Korea has shown little sign of reciprocating.

articles.title: What the Pentagon’s Sweeping Polygraph Hunt Has Revealed
articles.body:
Pentagon investigators administered polygraph tests to dozens of military officers and civilian employees in August as part of an investigation into disclosures about the nation’s dwindling weapons stockpiles.
The polygraph tests, first reported by The New York Times last week, followed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement in July that the Pentagon was forming a joint task force with the Department of Justice to identify and prosecute what he called the “unauthorized disclosure of sensitive” information to the press.
Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to TIME that the Pentagon does not comment on investigative matters but “takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”
“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” the statement said.
The August interrogations included some 50 members of the Joint Staff, according to the Times. CBS News also reported that several dozen officials were tested earlier this summer, including those from the U.S. Central Command.
Why did the Pentagon polygraph dozens of officials?
Sources familiar with the matter told multiple outlets this summer that U.S. supplies of certain critical munitions—including long-range precision-guided missiles and air-defense interceptors—had fallen dangerously low. They suggested that its inventory would likely dwindle further amid the ongoing war with Iran.
Sources told The Washington Post that Trump clashed with Hegseth over the matter during a visit to Camp David on July 31, claiming that he had been “misled on extreme munitions shortages that now threaten to limit military options with Iran.”
Trump refuted the idea that there were any shortages in a Truth Social post on Aug. 6.
“The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” Trump wrote in his post. “Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed.”
The President called for lengthy imprisonment for those caught leaking information to the press.
“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” he added. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”
In a separate post that same day, he denied that he’d fought with Hegseth, calling the reports “completely unfounded rumors.”
“I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing,” he said.
Trump intensified his attacks on the coverage on Sept. 3, calling media outlets who reported on the shortages “treasonous scum” who refuse to “accurately report” on the conflict with Iran.
Despite Trump’s repeated denials of a broad munitions shortage, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in late July that missile interceptor inventories have dropped—with Patriot inventories now under 1,000 and THAAD inventories at about 250.
Exact figures about the U.S. weapons cache are classified—and that’s for a good reason, according to Harrison Mann, a former defense intelligence official and a senior fellow with the advocacy group Win Without War.
“That is valuable information to any U.S. adversary,” he tells TIME. “Obviously, if they know that we're out of ammo in some significant way, it changes deterrence calculations for U.S. adversaries.”
At the same time, however, he argues that any shortage would likely be clear to the public and to Iran.
“Smart people can put together pretty accurate estimates of what the U.S. has used up between looking at what's been produced, which isn't necessarily a closely guarded secret, and looking at what has been expended on the battlefield,” he says. “Maybe not with the same amount of fidelity [as Pentagon officials], but the Iranians can tell when they're not getting hit by as many standoff munitions, and certainly everyone can tell when U.S. and partners have run out of interceptors.”
Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the CSIS Defense and Security Department, says he and his colleague created CSIS’s July report on dwindling munitions using only “unclassified” sources.
“If two people at a think tank can do this analysis with entirely unclassified sources, then the Chinese, with tens of thousands of intelligence operatives, and way better sources of information can get much better numbers,” Cancian says.
What Pentagon polygraph rules require—and what the tests found
The Pentagon adheres to specific guidelines and restrictions when administering polygraph tests. They are most commonly used in pre-employment and vetting for intelligence agencies like the National Security Agency and the Defense Intelligence Agency. They are also administered when personnel are seeking or maintaining access to top-secret, special-access, or other sensitive information—as well as in the event of unauthorized disclosures of classified information. 
Pentagon rules require an examinee’s written consent and allow the person to end the examination at any time. For an issue-specific counterintelligence examination, investigators must have interviewed the person, reasonably believe that the person knew about or was involved in the matter, pursue other investigative avenues as thoroughly as circumstances permit, and determine that the polygraph is essential to the investigation.
The Defense Secretary is also required to establish a process for monitoring the “responsible and effective” use of polygraphs and to make information about their use available to congressional defense committees.
The Pentagon has not released enough information to determine whether investigators followed all those requirements. It also has not disclosed the investigation’s findings. CBS News, however, reported that no one had failed the questions meant to determine whether any officials had leaked information to the media.
It also said that the polygraph tests included a wide range of questions pertaining to national security. Specifically, The New York Times reported that officials were asked if they had disclosed classified information to members of the press, according to information provided by its sources close to the investigation, and if they had provided information about diminished munitions stocks.
People familiar with the effort told the Times that the tests appeared intended not only to identify a leaker but also to deter officials who might leak classified information to the media in the future.
How unusual are polygraphs in Pentagon leak investigations?
While the use of polygraphs is not unheard of, the sheer number of people targeted during this investigation is uncommon, officials told CBS News.
David Pozen, a law professor at Columbia University, pointed TIME toward his article for the Harvard Law Review that assesses information leaks within the federal government.
“Periodically, task forces have recommended that the White House take concerted steps to facilitate leak investigations, such as regularizing the use of polygraphs and requiring government employees who speak with the press to provide advance notice, followed by summaries of what was discussed,” he wrote.
This was notably implemented during Ronald Reagan’s presidency in 1983. Reagan authorized polygraph testing in investigations of unauthorized classified disclosures, although he barred agencies from using the results alone to discipline employees.
Polygraphs have been considered or used in leak investigations under more recent administrations, as well. During the George W. Bush administration, the FBI interviewed nearly 100 members and staff of congressional intelligence committees while investigating leaked intelligence connected to the Sept. 11 attacks. Agents commonly asked whether they would take polygraphs, but most declined.
In subsequent years, publicly documented operations involving dozens of senior military officials appear exceedingly rare. But the Trump Administration has used polygraphs in previous leak investigations.
In early 2025, the Department of Homeland Security administered lie detector tests to identify people suspected of disclosing plans for immigration raids. That year, members of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s office were reportedly polygraphed in response to a leak investigation. At the direction of Director Kash Patel, the FBI also began using polygraphs in leak investigations in 2025. In a separate episode this year, more than two dozen current and former members of Patel’s security detail—in addition to some information-technology employees—were reportedly tested in an effort to identify sources of leaks about his leadership.
Still, Cancian says that polygraph use is more common at intelligence agencies than among senior military staff. He characterizes a polygraph hunt of this scale as incredibly unusual.
How the Pentagon’s polygraph hunt could affect future disclosures
While no leakers have been identified to the public, and it remains unknown whether the efforts uncovered any, the tests may serve a secondary purpose—which is to dissuade officials from sharing information in the future.
Cancian says the investigation stems from an “understandable” desire for senior Pentagon officials to have candid conversations with their employees without worrying about leaks to the press.
“Every administration is concerned about that. I think this one is particularly concerned about that,” Cancian says. Otherwise, officers may hesitate to put concerns in writing, circulate formal objections, or talk openly within authorized channels. The Joint Staff is tasked with giving civilian leaders candid assessments of readiness, risk, and operational sustainability, while coordinating with combatant commands around the world.
“Meetings get smaller and smaller, fewer and fewer people can attend because of concerns that larger groups, you know, might leak,” he says.
Mann adds that a polygraph test is known as an “inconclusive” tool.
“You can game them. You can get false positives,” he says. “So, you certainly won't necessarily get to the bottom of whatever you're searching for by running a lot of polygraphs, but it is quite effective as an intimidation tool and as a deterrent against leaks.”
He says that many officials are “still nervous” about doing routine polygraph tests, even if they have “nothing to hide.”
“They know it's something that you can fail and that can then disrupt your career or suspend your clearance if you can't pass it, even if it's just because you were nervous that day,” Mann continues.
He says that this polygraph hunt is a way for Hegseth to test the loyalty of his employees amid pressure over the continuation of efforts in Iran. Just this week, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina urged Trump to replace Hegseth as Defense Secretary.
“Independent of the Iran war, [Hegseth] has been trying quite hard, in my view, to streamline that bureaucracy to more personal loyalty—often at the expense of readiness or combat effectiveness,” Mann says. “This is one of the products of somebody who is trying to have a very, very tight grip on the bureaucracy he leads.”

articles.title: Ukrainian journalist asks Trump’s envoy to his face whether he was disgusted to sit across from “international criminal” Putin. Witkoff wouldn’t answer directly
articles.body:
At a Kyiv press conference on 6 September, Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Gordon asked US special envoy Steve Witkoff, to his face, whether he found it repugnant to sit across a table from Russian President Vladimir Putin. Witkoff did not answer directly, saying only that settling the war means keeping relations and communication open with both sides, according to Gordon.
US President Donald Trump began his peace efforts as soon as he returned to the White House in January 2025, promising to end the war in a single day. It did not happen. Instead, Russia has only stepped up its strikes on civilians and expanded the volume and types of weapons it uses for mass terror.
“And finally, aren’t you disgusted to be sitting at the same table with an international war criminal, the butcher of the Ukrainian people, who is personally responsible for the tragedy in Ukraine?” Gordon asked.
It is a reference with legal grounding, as the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023 over the deportation of Ukrainian children.
The questions Witkoff would not answer
Witkoff did not provide direct answers to the questions. He only added that, in order to resolve the war, it is important to maintain relations and communication with both sides of the conflict.
According to Trump’s special envoy, he has traveled to Moscow approximately eight times, where he met with Putin and his team, and said they "have always received respect from President Putin".
In practice, however, none of these meetings resulted in anything other than an intensification of the strikes. In the winter of 2025, a specific peace plan was discussed that, at the time, consisted of 20 points.
Yet as the discussions continued, Russia intensified its terror against civilians, destroying an entire thermal power plant in Kyiv and plunging millions of Kyiv residents and people in other cities into darkness amid temperatures as low as -15°C. Now, as the US is holding its anti-ballistic missile interceptors, this scenario will likely continue this winter.
“The language of force”
“Don’t you think that Putin, the Russians, and Russia understand only one language well — the language of force?” the journalist asked.
There was no direct answer to this question either. Instead, Witkoff said that their job is to bring the two sides together and improve communication.
Earlier, there have been numerous occasions when channels of communication between Russia and Ukraine have existed. This was confirmed by Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine and former intelligence chief, according to The New York Times.
Russia attempted to murder Gordon
In 2025, the Security Service of Ukraine said it had foiled an assassination attempt against journalist and media manager Gordon. According to the agency, the FSB of Russia was behind the plot to murder the prominent media figure.
According to investigators, the Russian intelligence service offered a $400,000 reward for carrying out the assassination.
As then-SBU chief Lieutenant General Vasyl Maliuk told journalists, Dmytro Gordon “triggers” Russians, while the Russian authorities regard him as Ukraine’s main “propagandist.”

articles.title: North Korea Commissions Kang Kon Destroyer That Capsized During 2025 Launch
articles.body:
North Korea has commissioned the Kang Kon destroyer into its navy, following its capsizing during an unsuccessful launch attempt last year.
The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported on this.
The commissioning ceremony took place on September 6 at the port of Wonsan on North Korea’s east coast. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended the event.
The destroyer is the second Choe Hyon-class warship and is going to join the Korean People’s Navy East Sea Fleet.
Despite being officially commissioned only now, the ship has already been used to demonstrate its combat capabilities. In early July 2026, it carried out a mass missile launch.
In addition to the missile launches, North Korean state media showed the ship’s onboard artillery systems firing.
In May 2025, during the ceremony to launch the ship from the slipway, the destroyer lost stability and tipped onto its side, damaging its hull.
The accident was captured in satellite imagery. North Korean state media also confirmed it.
Kim Jong Un, who attended the launch ceremony, said the accident was caused by negligence and irresponsibility that could be regarded as a criminal act.
He ordered the ship’s restoration to be completed by the June plenary meeting of the Workers’ Party of Korea and those responsible for shortcomings in its design and construction to be held accountable.
Following the failed launch, North Korean authorities arrested four officials, including the chief engineer, construction manager, and project administrative manager. They also detained Ri Hyong-son, a member of the Central Military Commission, whom the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) identified as one of the officials primarily responsible for the accident.
As early as June 2, 2025, satellite imagery captured the ship being raised while in an upright position.
On June 5, the destroyer was successfully launched and sent to a shipyard in Rajin for repairs. On June 8, the ship was moved into a dry dock to complete the restoration work.
The 5,000-ton Choe Hyon-class warships are multi-purpose missile destroyers of the Korean People’s Army Navy. They are equipped with two types of vertical launch systems: larger for strike weapons and smaller for air defense missiles. The ships have a total of 74 launch cells.
The ship’s artillery armament includes a 127 mm automatic gun, as well as a close-in weapon system that visually resembles the Soviet 30 mm AK-230 and AK-630 systems.
A North Korean anti-aircraft gun system located at the stern provides the ship’s air defense. Its appearance resembles that of the Russian Pantsir-M.
The anti-ship and strike weapons are housed in transport-launch containers on both sides of the ship. They likely include eight Hwasal-2 cruise missiles capable of engaging moving targets. In addition, each side is equipped with four launchers for a North Korean equivalent of the Spike ER/NLOS missiles.
Militarnyi previously reported that North Korean authorities had instructed shipbuilders to construct a new Choe Hyon-class destroyer within one year.

articles.title: Energy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with Iran
articles.body:
US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.
Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”
He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”.
He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports.
“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.
In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on.
This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area.
Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.
“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.
“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”
Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”
“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.
Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”.
Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.”
“But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added.
Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage.
Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.”
The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November.
“Probably not,” he said.
The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

articles.title: Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border
articles.body:
Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.
The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.
Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs
“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.
The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.
After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.
Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.
Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.
Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.
Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.
In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.
Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.
Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.
During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.
Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.
At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.
During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.
“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.

articles.title: Fire Point at the defense exhibition MSPO in Poland will showcase the FP-5 "Flamingo" and the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Fire Point at the defense exhibition MSPO in Poland will showcase the FP-5 "Flamingo" and the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles
Kyiv • UNN
Fire Point will present full-scale models of the FP-5 "Flamingo" at the MSPO 2026 exhibition in Poland, and will also discuss the Freyja project with European partners.
At the International Defence Industry Exhibition Międzynarodowy Salon Przemysłu Obronnego in Kielce, Poland, the Ukrainian company Fire Point will showcase full-size models of the FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missile and the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles. The company announced this, writes UNN.
Details
The 34th International Defence Industry Exhibition Międzynarodowy Salon Przemysłu Obronnego in Poland will take place from September 8 to 11. This year's MSPO will be the largest in the exhibition's history, with organisers expecting more than 1,000 participants from 40 countries. For the first time, the exhibition will also occupy the new Targi Kielce pavilion, covering an area of 15,500 m². The exhibition is held in cooperation with Poland's Ministry of National Defence and brings representatives of governments, military structures and the defence industry from dozens of countries to Kielce every year.
For Fire Point, this is an opportunity to join the dialogue about what defence should look like in conditions where the nature of warfare is changing faster than traditional weapons development and procurement cycles. Ukraine is already living in this reality. Massive missile and drone attacks, operations amid active electronic warfare, the constant changes in the enemy's tactics and the need to carry out long-range strikes are forcing Ukrainian manufacturers to rapidly adapt technologies and shorten the path from an idea to real-world application. It is precisely this experience that Fire Point will present in Kielce
At its stand, the Ukrainian defence technology company Fire Point will showcase full-size models of the FP-1 long-range UAV, the FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missile, as well as the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles.
In addition, at MSPO, Fire Point will continue discussions with European partners about the Freyja project – a pan-European antiballistic shield, for which the company is the chief architect and integrator.
That is why, for Fire Point, MSPO is primarily about negotiations, technological cooperation and partnerships that can give rise to new joint defence capabilities. Kielce is one of the places where discussions develop into cooperation
In addition
At the international MSPO 2026 exhibition in Kielce, Poland, Ukraine will be represented by at least 25 companies. Ukrainian manufacturers will showcase strike and reconnaissance drones, electronic warfare equipment, communications and cybersecurity systems, and other defence developments.
We remind you
The FP-5 "Flamingo" is a modern ground-based UAV/cruise missile system developed to deliver a specified payload of up to 1,150 kg to strike ground targets with fixed topographic coordinates at a range of up to 3,000 km, both day and night. The missile is capable of hitting a target even under conditions of active electronic interference.

articles.title: Report urges Britain to offer EU nuclear protection
articles.body:
Britain should explore what it calls a Deterrence Union with the European Union, formally extending its nuclear and conventional deterrent over the bloc in exchange for bespoke access to European defence funds, according to a report published by the Council on Geostrategy.
The paper, titled Towards a Hercules Hold: Maintaining a transatlantic defence industrial base, is written by Paul Mason and William Freer and carries a foreword by Tan Dhesi, the Labour MP for Slough and chair of the House of Commons Defence Committee.
Its central argument is that the transatlantic defence industrial base has begun to split, with Washington reprioritising resources towards hemispheric defence and countering China while the European Union deploys instruments such as the €150 billion SAFE facility in pursuit of strategic autonomy, and that those European mechanisms increasingly mandate the exclusion of third countries. Britain, sitting outside the European Union while maintaining deep security ties with Washington, is described as squeezed between two diverging defence giants and facing what the authors call a dangerous Hobson’s choice in capability standardisation.
The bridge has stopped working
The authors argue that the role Britain has traditionally assigned itself, acting as a transatlantic bridge, no longer serves the purpose it was designed for.
They write: “The historic approach of acting as a more passive transatlantic ‘bridge’ will prove insufficient to securing British interests. Instead, Britain should see itself as central to establishing a ‘Hercules hold’ to grip and sustain two diverging pillars. By focusing defence investment on select capabilities and championing interchangeability, HM Government can wield the influence necessary to maintain access to US technology while accelerating European rearmament.”
According to the report, further bifurcation risks cutting European allies off from cutting-edge American research and development along with North American surge capacity, leaving European nations with widening gaps in the high-end capabilities where the United States leads, among them ballistic missile defence, hypersonic strike and space systems, while integrated transatlantic defence firms face severe supply chain disruption.
What is being proposed
The Deterrence Union is the recommendation likely to attract most attention, since it would involve Britain formally offering nuclear protections to the European Union in return for deeper access to its defence market.
Alongside it the authors recommend championing hardware and munitions interchangeability across NATO, so that equipment can be physically swapped between allied platforms, and investing in a select portfolio of high-value technological chokepoints where British engineering becomes indispensable to both Washington and Brussels. They also call on the government formally to back the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank as a source of non-exclusionary funding for transatlantic projects.
Interchangeability is the same concept the First Sea Lord set out in an interview published last month, describing it as going beyond interoperability so that it becomes agnostic which nation is conducting a given task, with allied navies acting for each other’s collective requirements and able to exchange capabilities.
Why the timing matters
The report lands as the American review of force posture in Europe gets under way. Elbridge Colby, the Under Secretary of War for Policy, told a meeting in Brussels last week that the review would examine the strategic posture of American forces on the continent even as Washington prioritises the Western Hemisphere and the First Island Chain, and confirmed that allies had been sent a written questionnaire seeking their views.
British access to European defence funding instruments has been under negotiation since 2024, and the SAFE facility in particular has been the subject of argument over the terms on which non-member states can participate.
Dhesi, who wrote the foreword, pressed the Prime Minister at Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday to commit to a pathway to three per cent of gross domestic product on defence by 2030, telling the Commons that Britain faces a significantly increased threat level and a United States leadership for which European security is no longer a priority.
The Council on Geostrategy is a London-based think tank founded in 2021 which focuses on British foreign and defence policy, the Indo-Pacific, and the maritime and technological dimensions of national strategy. Paul Mason is a journalist and author who co-presents the organisation’s Defence Talks podcast.

articles.title: France Plans to Receive 47 Rafale F5 Fighters by 2035
articles.body:
The French Air and Space Force plans to receive 47 Rafale fighter jets in the latest F5 configuration by 2035.
This is set out in the updated French Military Programming Law (LPM) for 2024-2030.
The aircraft are primarily intended for France’s Strategic Air Forces (FAS), which carry out nuclear deterrence missions.
The Rafale F5 will be a significantly more comprehensive upgrade of the fighter than previous standards. The aircraft will receive new weapons control systems, an improved radar, electronic warfare systems, a new onboard defensive suite, new weapons, including MICA NG missiles, and improved data-link capabilities.
The Rafale F5 is also expected to be capable of carrying the future ASN4G hypersonic nuclear missile.
In addition to the aircraft itself, France is developing a combat drone designed to operate alongside the Rafale F5. The first development contracts have already been signed with Dassault Aviation, Thales and Safran.
The drone is intended to operate in complex environments, including suppressing enemy air defenses, and is to be used alongside Rafale F5 fighters.
However, despite France’s plans, the program to develop the new version of the aircraft is facing financial difficulties.
In April, it was reported that France would fully finance the development of the Rafale F5 after negotiations with the United Arab Emirates on joint financing of the program ended without an agreement.
The negotiations ended in December 2025. Paris proposed that Abu Dhabi join the program in exchange for investment, but without the participation of local companies in the development or the possibility of obtaining technology.
The UAE was expected to contribute up to €3.5 billion to the program, whose total cost is estimated at approximately €5 billion.
Following the UAE’s refusal, all financial commitments related to the program will be borne by the French Ministry of Defense, which could potentially affect the pace of its implementation.

articles.title: Iran vows 'painful response' as US sanctions squeeze economy
articles.body:
Iran said Sunday it will step up efforts to address problems caused by U.S. sanctions that have battered its economy, while a senior Iranian official warned that any further attack would draw a “painful response.”
Six months after U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran, the conflict appears to have reached a stalemate. A preliminary cease-fire agreement reached in June has unraveled, while diplomatic efforts to revive negotiations and restore a path toward peace have made little progress.
After a pause in military action through much of July, tit-for-tat attacks have resumed. U.S. Central Command said Saturday that it struck three Iranian tankers after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy ships.
Following the attacks, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said Sunday that the United States should understand that “the rules of the game” in the war against Iran have changed before it is too late.
Qalibaf’s warning came as Tehran faced mounting economic pressure from U.S. sanctions, which have severely restricted Iran’s access to international markets and deepened the challenges confronting its economy.
“From now on, any attack against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response,” he said in a speech published on his Telegram channel.
Tehran has shown it still retains the capability to attack U.S. interests in neighboring countries and to disrupt oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies flowed before the conflict.
However, the U.S. campaign to throttle Iran’s economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is becoming increasingly difficult to withstand, three senior Iranian sources said.
In his speech Sunday, Qalibaf added that alongside the military front, Iran’s main battle was now over production and people’s livelihoods.
He cited sharp currency fluctuations, inflation, unemployment and market management as major challenges, adding that Iranians could tolerate hardship but not mismanagement or inaction and expected the government to act quickly.
Iran’s Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran planned to respond to U.S. economic pressure with reforms and rejected the idea that sanctions would cause it to change course, according to state media Sunday.
“They speak of economic pressure and isolation, of breaking off financial ties, and they think that by pressuring the economy of a country they can change the decisions of its people,” Madanizadeh said.
“I have to clarify one point: The responsibility for reforming Iran’s economy is with its government and people, not with the U.S. Treasury.”
Separately, Economy Ministry Deputy Morteza Zamanian said Sunday that the ministry’s “Economic War Headquarters” was stepping up efforts to resolve problems caused by the war, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90% of its crude through its Kharg Island export hub before the war. Flows have been disrupted since a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.
On Aug. 31, Trump issued a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video depicting Kharg Island being “blown to smithereens.” Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.
In an interview aired on state TV Sunday, Iran’s oil minister, Mohsen Paknejad, said the island had been hit about 550 times in previous months but continued to operate.
Iran has also imposed a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, creating an issue for U.S. President Donald Trump by pushing up fuel prices globally ahead of the November midterm elections.
On Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it struck three Iranian vessels, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy ships.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost, taking out three of yours,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, which oversees U.S. military operations in the Middle East.
The IRGC responded by threatening intensified strikes against U.S. military vessels in the region and later said it had targeted the three tankers as well as three U.S.-linked vessels in other areas.
“Do not be deceived by the ‘terrorist’ U.S. military and refrain from any suspicious movement aimed at passing through unauthorized waterways,” the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried on Iranian state TV. “Otherwise, you will be targeted.”
Tasnim, the semi-official Iranian news agency, reported that four U.S. missiles hit a tanker in the area of Kharg’s anchorage. Tasnim quoted local sources as saying there were no casualties and the tanker’s crew was being evacuated.
No American personnel were harmed, Central Command said.
On Sunday, Tasnim reported that the IRGC had shot down a U.S. surveillance balloon over Erbil in northern Iraq, describing it as part of a broader effort to eliminate U.S. aerial surveillance and early-warning systems in the region.

articles.title: Kyiv stockpiles food and water as Russia’s new aerial tactics threaten a brutal winter
articles.body:
Kyiv is building reserves of food and drinking water to help residents during prolonged power outages and other emergencies, the Kyiv City Council said on 7 September.
The preparations come as Russia continues to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and food supply chains, while Ukrainian officials warn that water systems could also come under attack. Kyiv is therefore preparing for a broader range of disruptions this winter, not just power outages.
The city is preparing the reserves ahead of the 2026–2027 fall and winter season, with priority given to low-income residents and people facing difficult circumstances.
The supplies will also be available at Points of Invincibility, emergency support centers set up to provide basic services during prolonged blackouts, for people affected by emergencies, and for workers involved in emergency and other urgent response operations.
Kyiv prepares for attacks on food and water supplies as Russia makes air attacks harder to stop
Russia has increasingly targeted infrastructure connected to Ukraine’s food supply in recent months. Russian strikes have hit food warehouses and distribution facilities around Kyiv, contributing to shortages and periods of empty supermarket shelves in the capital and other parts of the country.
Ukrainian officials have also warned that Russia could target water infrastructure as part of its attacks on critical civilian systems, raising concerns about access to drinking water during prolonged disruptions.
This year, the threat is particularly acute as Russia has expanded its use of ballistic missiles and introduced faster, jet-powered Geran drones that are harder for Ukraine to intercept. Ballistic missiles can only be reliably intercepted by a limited number of air defense systems, while the faster drones reduce the time available to detect and engage them.
Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine’s modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped
Kyiv prepares for another difficult winter
Russia's strikes have repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure during previous winters, causing extended blackouts and disruptions to heating and other essential services.
Kyiv is now preparing for the possibility that attacks could again leave residents without electricity or access to essential supplies for extended periods.
Kyiv says food supply remains stable, for now
Oleh Kuіavskyi, deputy head of the Kyiv City State Administration, said the city's preparations are focused not only on accumulating supplies but also on ensuring they can quickly reach people who need them.
“Food security in the capital is not only about having the necessary reserves, but also a clear system for their distribution and delivery to those who need help most,” Kuіavskyi said, according to the Kyiv City Council.
He said Kyiv's consumer market remains stable and predictable, while the city continues to hold agricultural food fairs across its districts to help maintain access to basic food products.
Reserves could feed 25,000 people
According to the city council, Kyiv has already formed and is maintaining reserves of key food products for use if the energy system comes under severe strain.
With support from charitable and civic organizations, the city can organize hot meals for up to 25,000 people, officials said.
The city's Department of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development also plans to purchase another 20,000 food packages for use during emergencies.
The reserves are being coordinated through Kyiv's Humanitarian Headquarters, established in February 2022. The body coordinates the city administration, district administrations, municipal companies, charities, and donors, including the accounting and distribution of emergency resources.

articles.title: When the Fighting is Over: Will Ukraine War Vets Pose a Threat to European Security?
articles.body:
For Evgeniy Polishchuk, an injury brought an early end to the war in Ukraine. But coming home was only the beginning.
He remembers putting his khaki baseball cap on his wife’s head, a symbol he had finally returned, and holding his family in his arms. But very quickly, he understood that he would have to find his way in the world again – while his friends continued to fight.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I realized that although one chapter had ended for me personally, nothing had actually ended because many people were still defending my country,” he told TVP World.
Eventually, Polishchuk settled into a new rhythm in the southern Polish city of Kraków; just one of many Ukrainian veterans who have moved to the EU after completing their service.
Many more could follow in his footsteps when the war with Russia ends, and this has started to set alarm bells ringing in some European countries.
                                                                                                                                                                         
TVP World has confirmed that the police forces of Poland, Germany and Czechia, the three nations home to the largest Ukrainian populations in the EU, are jointly preparing an analysis of security threats that could emerge in the aftermath of the conflict.
Ukraine Counts on US Passing New Russia Sanctions, Zelensky Says
The possible arrival of battle-hardened Ukrainian veterans, many, perhaps, baring the psychological scars of combat, is considered one such threat.
In April, Czech police chief Martin Vondrášek said that influx of war veterans when the fighting stops poses “the biggest security risk for the Czech Republic that I perceive at this moment”.
But for others, these concerns are overblown and could be exploited by hostile actors eager to fuel fear and resentment against Ukrainians living in the EU.
‘We must be prepared’
The details of the analysis being prepared by Poland, Germany and Czechia remain closely guarded.
The Czech Police confirmed to TVP World the existence of the joint assessment, saying the three countries were “preparing an analysis of security threats that may arise after the end of the war in Ukraine”.
However, they said the document was still being worked on and had not reached its final form.
The Polish Police also confirmed it was working with its Czech and German counterparts, but said it would not comment on the “work and analyses” being carried out as part of the “trilateral cooperation”.
Nevertheless, it pointed to several ways the end of the conflict could create security risks for neighboring nations.
“After the end of the war beyond our eastern border, there is a risk that the demobilization process will contribute to the growth of organized crime, a real and historically proven phenomenon,” the Polish Police told TVP World.
It warned of increased weapons trafficking, drug smuggling, extortion and money laundering, as well as recruitment of veterans by criminal groups.
“War corrupts, and those with combat experience often face enormous difficulties returning to civilian life,” it said. “We must be prepared for various scenarios in the period after the end of the war in Ukraine.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
That preparation extends beyond conventional crime.
Poland, as a “key logistical hub” for aid and support to Ukraine, has become particularly exposed to sabotage, disinformation and cybercrime, the police added.
It argued the answer is to prepare before the threats materialize, for example by creating a new National Police Investigation Bureau to tackle organized crime.
The Polish Police said its approach was based on “hard statistical data, not generalizations or stereotypes”, and pointed to the experience of previous conflicts in the Balkans and Afghanistan.
It added that it would monitor the potential presence of veterans “with full professional attention”, while ensuring that the military community is not stigmatized.
War’s toll
Andriy Kucher, a Ukrainian war veteran, acknowledges that some former combatants will struggle with PTSD, substance abuse or aggression in civilian life. He told TVP World this will be “a huge challenge” for them in the years ahead but believes the problem will not be widespread.
“Mostly it’s normal people who want to have a peaceful life,” he stressed. “They want to go back to their family or have some quiet place to stay alive and just live their lives.”
Kucher had been fighting near Marinka in Ukraine’s Donetsk region when a sniper narrowly missed him and killed his commander. Later that same day a missile struck his position; he was wounded, while his 23-year-old friend died in his arms.
                                                                                                                                                                         
That day, he says, was a turning point – a brutal reminder of how quickly life can change, but also of what he had to be grateful for.
He later set up Strong 300, an organization supporting wounded soldiers and veterans through community, rehabilitation and sport. Rebuilding his own life became inseparable from helping others rebuild theirs.
Yana Chapailo, director of the Ukrainian Defenders Leadership Center, which works with veterans to strengthen their leadership potential, rejects the idea that veterans pose a collective security threat.
“I would not put veterans and criminals in the same sentence,” she told TVP World.
Any crimes they commit should be dealt with by the police on a case-by-case basis, she says. But “you cannot take the behaviour of individual people and apply it to millions of those who are defending their country”.
‘Harmful clichés’ and propaganda
The concern is that fears about Ukrainian veterans could be deliberately amplified by foreign actors to drive a wedge between Ukrainians and their neighbors.
“I think all Europeans need to understand that this is all part of a hybrid war,” Kucher said. “And Russians, unfortunately, are the best at propaganda.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
For Maria Piechowska, an analyst at the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), this socio-political lens is the most concerning.
“The police, the Polish state has its tools to fight the security issues,” she told TVP World. “But if we talk about disinformation, if we talk about Russian propaganda, we are not so well prepared.”
She pointed out that Polish-Ukrainian relations have already been vulnerable to political disputes and Russian disinformation, and that just a handful of incidents involving veterans would provide fresh material for turning public opinion against Ukrainians.
Iryna Dobrohorska, an expert from Adam Smith International, a global advisory company, warns that a lack of available data could augment the problem.
Millions of Ukrainian women and children have already moved to Europe, creating a potential pull factor for veterans.
But it is too early to estimate how many would move, Dobrohorska said, because much will depend on how the war ends, as well as factors like employment opportunities abroad and the EU’s temporary protection scheme.
“What I am worried about is the matter of veterans becoming politicized,” Dobrohorska told TVP World. “Without any grounded data, that may become a major risk.”
Piotr Łukasiewicz, Poland’s chargé d’affaires in Ukraine, has previously warned that European governments need to be very careful about how they the approach the issue.
“The worst thing we could do… would be to succumb to harmful clichés,” he said, warning against claims that Ukrainian veterans will “set up mafias” or become a criminal or drug problem after the war.
“We must understand this phenomenon and participate in it, rather than frighten ourselves with it,” he added.
Opportunity, not threat
Asked about the security plans Poland, Germany and Czechia are preparing, the Ukrainian Veterans’ Ministry stressed that those defending the country are among the people most invested in a peaceful and secure future.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“Most veterans came into military service from civilian life – they were entrepreneurs, engineers, doctors, IT specialists and teachers,” the ministry told TVP World. “Many will return to these professions, build businesses and continue contributing to their communities after service.”
For Chapailo, the war-vets wets should be seen as an asset rather than a threat.
“They’ve already established that they have numerous tools and expertise in their hands,” she said. “They are resourceful, they are fast in decision-making, they’ve survived the war.”
She pointed to one former prisoner of war who spent two and a half years in Russian captivity. While imprisoned, he made a mental list of what he wanted to do when he returned. One ambition was to teach.
After coming home, Chapailo helped him become a tutor for other veterans, sharing his expertise in analytics.
“That was his plan when he was sitting in his cell,” Yana told TVP World. “And right now he’s working with these veterans.”
Kucher argues that far from being a threat, Ukrainian veterans could enhance European security, for example by passing on their knowledge of high-tech warfare to the militaries of their adopted homelands.
“The world has changed and each country must rebuild their own security as soon as possible,” he says. “Our unique experience can be useful for you.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry has said previously that veterans are “not a threat, but a security factor for Ukraine, Poland and the whole of Europe.”
“We are convinced that the brave Ukrainian men and women who stood up to defend their country and the world against Russian invaders deserve the highest respect.”
The challenge, then, is not simply how to manage veterans returning to civilian life, but how to make sure their experience is not lost.
“We have to think about a challenge, but not a problem,” Piechowska told TVP World, suggesting that ex-combatants could also be extremely useful in emergency services. “We have to think about opportunity and how we can use their skills.”
So, what next?
None of this means security risks can simply be ignored.
Asked about concerns from Ukrainian veterans and trusts, Poland’s Interior Ministry told TVP World that ensuring public safety and monitoring the consequences of the war are its “absolute priority”.
“We are considering various scenarios, including the risk associated with the illicit trade in weapons and ammunition, and the increased activity of organized crime groups,” the ministry said.
It added that it was continuously sharing information with Ukraine, including cooperation between police and border services.
                                                                                                                                                                         
But experts and veterans argue that preparation should extend well beyond policing.
The challenge of helping ex-combatants return to civilian life will be greatest in Ukraine itself, which is already building a system to support them, covering healthcare, rehabilitation, mental health, housing and much more.
For Kucher, European countries could help expand these efforts rather than waiting until veterans move to the EU.
He argues for dedicated funding programs for veterans, separate to wider humanitarian resources, and had a simple message for governments looking for practical ways to help.
“You need to support veteran NGOs,” he says. “We already work with wounded soldiers. Each week I visit wounded soldiers in hospital, and I understand them and what they need the most.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Piechowska agrees that preparation needs to start early, and that EU states will also need to invest in their own healthcare systems, but she stresses preparation is not only about services. It is also about communication.
She argues that European governments need to think now about how veterans will be discussed in public and how to prevent legitimate concerns becoming a source of social division.
That means developing a “conscious communication policy”, she says, alongside better media and cyber literacy.
Living without fear
After several years away from the frontline, Polishchuk has found a home in Polish society, rebuilding a life close to his family while working, building a business and remaining useful.
In a Kraków restaurant not long ago, he met a young Polish man who was looking for work. There was nothing available, so Polishchuk gave him 100 złoty (€23). The man asked where he was from.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“I told him I’m from Ukraine. And his immediate question was, why aren’t you fighting?”
Polishchuk explained that he was a war veteran who had fought, but was now rebuilding his civilian life in Poland.
The young man was surprised. The veteran had followed him into the street not to ask for help, but to offer it.
“Sometimes society itself, it’s not fully prepared for veterans to return,” Polishchuk told TVP World. “There is an enormous difference between the life experience of someone who has been through a war and someone who has not.”
His principle is straightforward: “A veteran should absolutely be treated as an equal member of society. Not as a victim and not as someone who will come to Europe needing assistance or creating a problem.
“A veteran can be someone who works, builds businesses, participates in society, and helps other people.”
