articles.title: Turkey pushes KAAN stealth jet as tensions with Israel deepen
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey pushes KAAN stealth jet as tensions with Israel deepen
Turkey is accelerating development of its fifth-generation KAAN fighter jet as Ankara seeks greater military independence amid increasingly open tensions with Israel and Israeli strikes targeting potential Turkish military expansion in Syria.
The Turkish-built fighter is intended eventually to provide Ankara with a sovereign alternative to the US-made F-35, a programme Turkey was expelled from after acquiring Russia's S-400 air defence system.
Turkey had been a partner in the F-35 programme and planned to operate the stealth fighter before Washington removed Ankara and later imposed sanctions over the S-400 purchase.
The setback left Turkey without an operational fifth-generation fighter, while Israel operates the F-35I Adir, giving it a significant advantage in stealth air power.
KAAN, developed by Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAS), is intended to narrow that gap while reducing Ankara's dependence on foreign suppliers for advanced military capabilities.
The aircraft's first prototype flew in February 2024, while a newer prototype began taxi tests in July as Turkey moves towards a more advanced phase of testing.
Turkish officials say the aircraft was designed domestically from the ground up as part of a decades-long effort to establish an independent combat aircraft industry.
KAAN is being developed with stealth, internal weapons carriage, advanced radar, electronic warfare and sensor fusion.
These technologies intend to make the aircraft harder to detect and allow pilots to combine information from multiple sensors into a single battlefield picture.
However, one of the programme's biggest remaining challenges is the engine.
KAAN's prototypes and initial production aircraft rely on US-made General Electric F110 engines.
Turkey is developing the TF35000, a domestic 35,000-pound-thrust-class engine intended eventually to power KAAN, but Turkish Aerospace has indicated that integration is targeted for around 2032.
Developing an advanced fighter engine is particularly difficult because it requires technologies including heat-resistant alloys, turbine cooling, precision manufacturing and sophisticated digital controls.
Until Turkey succeeds, KAAN will reduce some forms of foreign dependence while retaining another through its reliance on US propulsion.
Israeli aggression raises the stakes
That vulnerability has become more significant as relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated.
Syria has emerged as a major arena of tension since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 and the emergence of a new government closely aligned with Ankara.
In April 2025, Israel struck the T4, Palmyra and Hama airbases after Turkish military teams had inspected the facilities as Ankara considered expanding its military presence in Syria.
Sources told Reuters at the time that the attack rendered T4 effectively unusable, with one regional intelligence official describing the strikes as a message that Israel would not accept an expanded Turkish presence.
Tensions escalated further in August, when Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria after claiming Turkish troops were preparing to deploy there.
Turkey and Syria denied that any permanent Turkish deployment was planned.
US envoy Tom Barrack later said US intelligence had examined the Israeli claim and concluded that Turkey was not moving military assets into the base.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has nevertheless warned that Israel would not tolerate an expanding Turkish military presence in Syria.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also warned President Recep Tayyip Erdogan against what he described as "dangerous" military moves in Syria and against testing Israel's willingness to act.
Israel has also opposed Turkey regaining access to the F-35.
Netanyahu said in July that he opposed a possible US sale of the aircraft to Ankara, arguing that it could alter the regional balance of power.
President Donald Trump has signalled a willingness to reconsider Turkey's access to the F-35, although political and legal obstacles remain.
For Ankara, Israel's fifth-generation air advantage, its strikes on Syrian military infrastructure linked to possible Turkish deployments and its opposition to Turkey acquiring F-35s add further strategic importance to KAAN.
A mature KAAN equipped with a Turkish engine, radar, electronic warfare systems and weapons would give Ankara a degree of independent high-end air power it currently lacks.
Israel, however, already operates a mature and combat-tested F-35 fleet, while KAAN remains in development.
Turkey is also seeking foreign partners for the programme, with Saudi Arabia in advanced discussions over possible involvement.
If Ankara succeeds in combining KAAN with a domestically produced engine and indigenous combat systems, the fighter could significantly reduce Turkey's reliance on Washington while beginning to narrow one of Israel's most important technological advantages over it.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Hitting Airfield, Major Oil Refinery and Air Defenses
articles.body:

Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Hitting Airfield, Major Oil Refinery and Air Defenses
Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don airfield, the Ryazan Oil Refinery, and three Russian air defense assets during an overnight operation in Russia on September 6, with fires reported at both the airfield and refinery.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 6, Ukrainian forces targeted the Ryazan Oil Refinery in Russia’s Ryazan region. A fire was recorded at the facility, which the General Staff said is involved in supplying the Russian armed forces.
The Ryazan refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, with a design capacity of around 17 million metric tons of crude per year. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, and other petroleum products.
Fire Point, a Ukrainian defense manufacturer, said its FP-1 drones struck equipment at two major primary crude-processing units at the refinery.
The company reported hits on the distillation columns of the ELOU-AVT-6 unit, the refinery’s largest primary processing unit with an annual capacity of 8.5 million metric tons, as well as equipment at the AVT-3 unit, which has a capacity of 3.1 million tons per year.
Together, the two units account for more than 77% of the refinery’s primary oil-processing capacity, according to Fire Point.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don airfield in Russia’s Rostov region. The General Staff reported a fire in the area of the facility but said the extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Three Russian air defense assets were also hit in the Rostov region—a Podlet radar station and two Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems.
The Podlet radar is designed to detect low-altitude and small aerial targets, including drones and cruise missiles. The Pantsir-S1 is a short-range air defense system combining surface-to-air missiles with 30 mm automatic cannons to engage aircraft, helicopters, drones, and precision-guided weapons.
The strikes were part of a broader overnight Ukrainian drone operation that targeted at least 14 Russian regions, as well as temporarily occupied Crimea and areas over the Black and Azov seas. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed 258 Ukrainian drones were intercepted, while Moscow and the surrounding region were left untouched under a temporary airspace arrangement during US envoy visits.

articles.title: Trump official says ‘there may not be a nuclear agreement’ with Iran
articles.body:
Trump official says ‘there may not be a nuclear agreement’ with Iran
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright’s comments could signal that US hopes for a nuclear deal are dimming.
As the United States and Iran resume trading attacks, a top US official has publicly downplayed the chances of one of President Donald Trump’s initial key objectives in the US and Israel’s war on Iran: getting a signed nuclear agreement.
During an interview on Sunday with US channel ABC News, the US Energy Secretary, Chris Wright, said “there may not” be a nuclear deal, signalling that the US may pivot instead to launching strikes against any Iranian efforts to build nuclear infrastructure.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
- list 2 of 3Iran President Pezeshkian calls for unity as US ramps up economic pressure
- list 3 of 3US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
“It may be simply destroying their capabilities to do it,” Wright said on ‘ABC This Week’ about Iran’s ambitions to obtain a nuclear weapon.
The US has previously targeted facilities it said had been used to support Iran’s nuclear programme. Iran has always maintained that it is developing a nuclear power programme only and does not have plans to build a nuclear weapon.
Later, when pressed by the show’s co-host, Martha Raddatz, on whether the US would resort to continued bombing instead of diplomacy, Wright defended US actions in Iran.
“They don’t have the capability to build more missiles,” Wright said. “We’re degrading their capacity to develop nuclear weapons and, ultimately, to deliver them if they develop them.”
However, the former oil executive whose agency oversees the US stockpile of nuclear weapons said that a deal with Iran could be possible under new leadership.
“An agreement may await the next administration in Iran,” he said. “We simply don’t know that.”
The Trump administration official’s comments could signal that US hopes for a nuclear deal are dimming and slipping further out of reach.
After the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran collapsed in July, attacks paused, then resumed, coupled with Iranian closures of the Strait of Hormuz and US naval blockade.
Despite recent exchanges of intense fire between US and Iranian forces, the White House has attempted to minimise the conflict in public remarks.
On Friday, Trump sought to downplay the war in Iran, calling it “small potatoes”. While at a White House news briefing on Thursday, Vice President JD Vance appeared to suggest that the conflict had cooled and to shrug off an alleged US attack on a wedding in southern Iran, saying “sometimes things happen“.
At a White House briefing this week, Vance said of the conflict that he “wouldn’t call it a war” and there was “no active shooting right now”.
Without offering specifics, Wright on Sunday said the US would “get the job done” in Iran and other nations would be offering their help to bring an end to the war.
“We will work in cooperation with our allies in the region,” Wright said. “I think you’ll see countries from around the world joining this effort as well.”
Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: China calls itself neutral—but its fiber ends up in the drones that hit Ukraine
articles.body:
Shipping documents show how a Chinese state company kept supplying Russia's drone factories with the raw material used in its long-range attack drones, Politico reported. Chinese parts have been recovered from downed Russian drones before. These records are the first to show the raw material shipped straight to the factory—a sanctioned arm of Russia's nuclear giant Rosatom.
Russia's mass-produced attack drones run on parts sourced worldwide that keep slipping past Western export controls, and Ukrainian cities take the hits almost nightly. Kyiv has spent the war naming the foreign suppliers behind that hardware, one component at a time.
What the documents show
The papers trace 46 metric tons of carbon-fiber chemicals from Jilin Chemical Fiber Group to Alabuga-Volokno, a Rosatom subsidiary in Tatarstan. The exporter disguised the cargo under a customs code meant for civilian fibers like nylon, said weapons expert David Albright, who studies Russia's drone production. That precursor, polyacrylonitrile, is the raw ingredient for the light carbon fiber in Russia's Shahed-type attack drones.
Drones of that type killed at least 15 people at a shopping mall in central Ukraine in August. Albright estimated the load could yield enough for as many as 1,300 kamikaze drones. The Kyiv-based Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, a think tank close to Ukraine's government, gathered the documents and shared them with Western governments. The US House Select Committee on China judged them legitimate, and Ukraine confirmed their authenticity.
Why Beijing can't plead ignorance
Alabuga-Volokno has faced Western sanctions since 2023 from the US, UK, EU, Ukraine, and others. Jilin faces none. Albright said the documents would let the State Department sanction the Chinese supplier. Serhii Kuzan, who heads the Ukrainian center, called China arguably the main and only source of these composite materials.
Former US officials rejected any idea that Beijing was unaware.
"The idea that Chinese state-owned enterprises can hide things from the Chinese government just doesn't wash," said Dennis Wilder, a former CIA deputy assistant director for East Asia and the Pacific.
Denials and a summit
Rosatom claimed it works in full compliance with the law. China's embassy in Washington called the evidence an attempt to "smear and scapegoat China," saying Beijing has never supplied lethal weapons.
The disclosure lands as US President Donald Trump prepares to meet Xi Jinping in Washington this month. In late August, Xi told Vladimir Putin their ties were set to strengthen.

articles.title: Russia Deliberately Fired Kh-101 Into Poland to Test NATO’s Red Lines, Ukraine’s Intelligence Chief Says

Russia Deliberately Fired Kh-101 Into Poland to Test NATO’s Red Lines, Ukraine’s Intelligence Chief Says
Ukraine’s military intelligence believes that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile that struck Poland on July 30 was deliberately directed into NATO territory as part of Moscow’s effort to test the Alliance’s response to a potential armed attack.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an interview with Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko published by Ukrinform on September 7.
“The trajectory of the missile differed from the trajectory of the group of missiles launched at Ukrainian territory from the very beginning of its flight, which indicates the deliberate nature of the actions,” Ivashchenko said.
He said Ukrainian intelligence possesses materials indicating broader aggressive intentions by Russia toward Europe and assessed the July incident as an attempt by Moscow to test NATO’s “red lines” regarding collective defense in the event of an armed attack against an Alliance member.
Ivashchenko said Russia has been unable to achieve its objectives in its war against Ukraine and is therefore considering escalating its confrontation with countries on NATO’s eastern flank in an effort to pressure European governments into reducing military support for Kyiv.
Ukraine’s military intelligence is tracking Russian violations of NATO members’ airspace, including Poland, Romania and the Baltic states, as well as military provocations near NATO borders, sabotage against European critical infrastructure, false-flag operations, cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns.
Ivashchenko warned that Russia is expected to further increase pressure on NATO’s eastern flank to test the response of Alliance members and portray them as unwilling to enter into an open confrontation with Moscow.
According to him, such actions are also intended to increase psychological pressure on European countries and ultimately undermine their military assistance to Ukraine.
Earlier, Poland announced it would temporarily restrict air traffic along its eastern border from September 10 to December 9 to give its air defense systems greater freedom to respond to potential Russian threats.

articles.title: North Korea deploys warship ‘capable of annihilating retaliatory strikes’
articles.body:
North Korea deploys warship ‘capable of annihilating retaliatory strikes’
Leader Kim Jong Un says vessel will form part of Pyongyang’s nuclear response system, strengthen naval forces.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended the commissioning of a warship he said could deliver “annihilating retaliatory strikes on an enemy”, citing “constant threats”, according to the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The Kang Kon, named after the North Korean military leader who was killed in action during the Korean War, was formally deployed at a ceremony at the eastern Wonsan Port in Kangwon Province on Sunday.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3North Korea’s Kim orders navy to build 10,000-tonne destroyer: State media
- list 3 of 3North Korea fires ballistic missiles as US-South Korea drills near end
In his address, Kim said the warship “represents the self-respect and will” of North Korea to defend its rights and interests, KCNA reported.
“The time has come for us to exercise our sovereignty at sea and under water,” Kim said, according to KCNA.
He said that “dangerous shadows must be erased” and that North Korea was under constant threat in the “sea east of the Korean Peninsula and nearby waters”, KCNA reported.
KCNA did not specify what weapons systems might be deployed on the Kang Kon, but said it has the same weapons systems as the 5,000-tonne warship Choe Hyon launched in June.
A previous KCNA report said Choe Hyon-class destroyers can carry a range of weapons, including missiles that analysts say are capable of carrying a nuclear payload.
The ship was commissioned a day before the US, South Korea and Japan were set to begin a five-day military exercise in waters east and south of South Korea’s Jeju Island.
South Korea’s military said in a statement that the Freedom Edge exercise is defensive in nature and meant to respond to North Korean nuclear and missile threats as well as promote regional peace and stability.
North Korea has previously slammed the trilateral drill as a “reckless show of strength”.
Sunday marks the third launch of the Kang Kon; the destroyer partially capsized during the first commissioning in May 2025 before it was repaired and relaunched the following month. It underwent further repairs and sea trials before completing weapons testing in July this year.
Kim said he would demonstrate another stage of North Korea’s naval buildup in eight months, KCNA said, without giving details.
North Korea has accelerated efforts to modernise its navy as Kim pursues a broader expansion of the country’s nuclear-capable forces.
He also said the construction of naval bases on North Korea’s east coast was under way and that the country would create new naval units and build different classes of warships.
Pyongyang, which calls itself an “irreversible” nuclear state, frames the build-up as deterrence against Washington and Seoul. The Korean Peninsula remains technically at war, and Kim has accused the allies of driving the region “to the brink of a nuclear war”.

articles.title: Chinese State Firm Secretly Sent Russia 46 Tons of Carbon-Fiber Materials for Strike Drones
articles.body:

Chinese State Firm Secretly Sent Russia 46 Tons of Carbon-Fiber Materials for Strike Drones
A Chinese state-owned company supplied Russia with materials needed to manufacture hundreds of strike drones, according to internal Russian shipping records obtained by POLITICO on September 4.
The documents, which have also been reviewed by Western governments, offer evidence to date that a Chinese state-controlled company has continued supplying a sanctioned enterprise linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Shipping and customs records show that earlier this year, the Chinese company sent 46 metric tons of carbon-fiber-related chemicals to a subsidiary of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom. According to POLITICO, the shipment was declared under a customs classification typically used for materials such as nylon and polyester.
The Rosatom subsidiary develops critical components for strike drones used by Russia in attacks against Ukraine, including a strike on a shopping mall in central Ukraine in August that killed at least 16 people.
Chinese-made components have previously been found in Russian drones recovered after attacks on Ukraine. However, the newly obtained records reportedly provide the first detailed evidence of a Chinese state-owned company directly exporting essential drone-production materials to Russia.
The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre (USCC), a Kyiv-based think tank, uncovered the documents through Russian sources and subsequently shared them with the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States.
David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security, said the records could provide grounds for the US State Department to sanction the Chinese supplier, as they document shipments to the Rosatom subsidiary after it had been sanctioned by several Western countries.
“Rosatom and its enterprises operate in full compliance with applicable laws and regulatory requirements,” said a spokesperson for the Russian state firm. “Any claim to the contrary is false and demonstrates a lack of understanding of how Russia’s customs authorities operate.”
The reported shipments come amid growing scrutiny of Chinese companies accused of supporting Russia’s war effort. The European Union’s diplomatic service has been seeking sanctions against four Chinese companies over their alleged involvement in supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The companies were expected to be included in the EU’s next sanctions package. Officials said their alleged activities included supporting Russia’s shadow fleet, supplying chemicals used by the Russian military, and providing components for the production of attack drones.
The proposed measures were outlined in a May 21 document and formed part of a smaller sanctions package that two EU officials said was expected to be approved by foreign ministers at a meeting in Luxembourg on June 15.

articles.title: Satellite Imagery Confirms Damage to Millerovo Air Base
articles.body:
Satellite imagery has confirmed damage to two radars, the technical and operational unit and an ammunition depot at Millerovo air base in the Rostov region.
Satellite images showing the aftermath of the attack were published by the Dnipro OSINT project’s channel.
The attack was carried out overnight on August 30 by the 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces using FP-1 drones. Millerovo and Yeysk air bases were targeted in the attack.
According to the satellite imagery, an ammunition depot, RSP-27 and Nebo-SV radars, and the technical and operational unit were damaged at Millerovo air base. The unit and ammunition depot were completely destroyed.
Millerovo military air base, located 170 kilometers from the line of contact, is used by Russian forces to launch Shahed-type strike drones and carry out airstrikes.
Millerovo air base is known to host the Russian 31st Fighter Aviation Regiment of the Russian Aerospace Forces, equipped with Su-30SM and Su-35 fighter jets.
The destroyed RSP-27 is an airfield surveillance radar that, in addition to detecting aerial targets, is an integral element of air traffic control.
The serious damage to the airfield’s technical and operational unit could also complicate preparations of Russian aircraft for sorties.
With the development of long-range drones, Millerovo is increasingly becoming a target of Ukrainian attacks. Several days before the 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces carried out its attack. The Long-Range Strike Company of the 429th Unmanned Systems Brigade Achilles published a video of a strike.
At the time, Ukrainian troops used a RAM-2X strike drone to hit a Nebo-U radar station in the Rostov region. Ahead of the strike, a Ukrainian reconnaissance UAV conducted aerial reconnaissance of the site.
Several days earlier, the 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces hit a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet at Millerovo air base.
In late August, Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the Russian Akhtubinsk military air base in the Astrakhan region, where a Su-34 frontline bomber was damaged.

articles.title: Sayyari: Iran’s deterrence capabilities have significantly increased after recent wars
articles.body:
Sayyari: Iran’s deterrence capabilities have significantly increased after recent wars
TEHRAN — Iran’s deterrence capabilities have significantly strengthened following the country’s recent military confrontations with the United States and Israel, Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, deputy chief of Iran’s Army for Coordination Affairs, said.
Reacting to recent remarks by US President Donald Trump about maintaining pressure on Iran, Sayyari said Washington’s statements reflected its inability to achieve its objectives on the battlefield.
He said strengthening Iran’s deterrence remained a central responsibility of the Armed Forces and that the military had drawn on its experience in recent conflicts to identify weaknesses and reinforce its capabilities.
“Based on the valuable experiences gained from the 12-day war jointly imposed by the United States and Israel against Iran, as well as the subsequent 40-day conflict, including what we refer to as the Ramadan War and the Hormuz War, we have made extensive efforts to address potential weaknesses and strengthen our capabilities,” Sayyari said.
“These efforts have significantly increased the country’s deterrence power,” he added.
Sayyari was also dismissive of Trump’s remarks about a possible naval and economic blockade of Iran, describing them as unfounded and repetitive.
He said Trump had repeatedly made similar claims about Iran, including that the country did not possess nuclear weapons, that its navy and air force had been destroyed, and that its economy was in severe difficulty.
“We have become accustomed to these unfounded and baseless statements,” Sayyari said.
The senior commander said US officials were well aware of Iran’s military capabilities and argued that Washington would not be able to overcome 'the combat power, resistance and national resolve of the Iranian people.'
“As long as the people remain united and stand alongside the government officials, no one can defeat Iran,” he said.
Sayyari pointed to Iran’s eight-year war with Iraq, from 1980 to 1988, known in Iran as the Sacred Defense, as a historical example of 'the Iranian people’s resilience under sustained military pressure.'
He also praised 'the continued support of the Iranian people for the Islamic Republic,' describing national unity and public resilience as important elements of Iran’s deterrence.

articles.title: Russia’s Budget Deficit Surges to $82 Billion as Ukrainian Strikes Hammer War Economy

Russia’s Budget Deficit Surges to $82 Billion as Ukrainian Strikes Hammer War Economy
Ukraine’s strikes against targets deep inside Russia are increasingly damaging Moscow’s ability to sustain its war effort and contributing to a federal budget deficit that has reached $82 billion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In an interview with Ukrinform published on September 7, Chief of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Oleh Ivashchenko said Ukrainian strikes are forcing Russia to halt production, repair damaged facilities, alter logistics, redeploy air defense systems, and spend additional resources.
“Our strikes are contributing to the growth of the Russian Federation’s budget deficit, which today stands at $82 billion,” Ivashchenko said.
He described the impact of Ukrainian attacks on Russia as “very critical,” saying Ukraine is targeting energy infrastructure that supplies Russian forces with fuel, logistics hubs, and facilities supporting the country’s military-industrial complex.
Ivashchenko said the broader objective of the campaign is not simply to demonstrate how far Ukrainian weapons can reach, but to reduce Russia’s capacity to manufacture weapons, supply its forces, and continue the war.
Russia’s finances have come under increasing pressure as the war continues. On September 3, Russian leader Vladimir Putin acknowledged that the country’s budget deficit was growing but insisted it remained manageable. Russia’s deficit reached 2.8% of GDP in January through July, while the government’s official target for the full year remains 1.6%.
Ivashchenko also said Russia is now significantly weaker economically than it was at the beginning of the full-scale invasion, pointing to labor shortages, the expanding federal budget deficit, and worsening conditions in the banking sector.
Despite those pressures, Ukrainian intelligence assesses that Moscow still possesses enough resources to continue its war against Ukraine, potentially through 2027 and 2028.
Ivashchenko said further pressure—including Ukrainian strikes, sanctions, and efforts to restrict Russia’s access to foreign components, technologies, and industrial equipment—would be needed to further erode Moscow’s ability to finance and sustain the war.
Earlier, Russia’s central bank gold reserves fell to their lowest level in more than six years as Moscow increasingly relied on liquid reserve assets to meet rising budget demands.

articles.title: Russia’s FM says war must end so there is “no more Nazism” in Europe. Russian occupation official already said what that means: erasing Ukraine and stopping its aid
articles.body:
Russia's foreign minister says the war has to end so that "no more Nazism" is left in Europe. Sergei Lavrov made the claim in a speech to students, casting Russia's war once again as a fight against a Nazi threat.
Earlier, Aleksei Selivanov, a sanctioned collaborator who became a senior official in the occupation administration of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, revealed the meaning behind the term "denazification". "Denazification is re-Russification," he said, adding that where Russian troops arrive, Ukrainian nationhood "ceases to exist," according to United24.
Russia reportedly points on Germany, one of Ukraine's main supporters
Meanwhile, Andrii Kovalenko, Head of the National Security and Defense Council's Center for Countering Disinformation, linked Lavrov's statement to the recent conflict between Germany and Russia over the drone attack on Ukraine's plane in Leipzig.
"Russia’s aggression is now becoming even more overt, with the main focus being placed on the political dismantling of the current elites who refused to acknowledge this aggression right under their noses," Kovalenko said.
Germany has been a long-term supporter of Ukraine, sending tons of aid, including Gepard anti-drone guns and Leopard tanks.
Russia plans Ukraine's new power figures after the war
"This war must be ended so that there is no more Nazism in Europe, which has again spread its metastases here," Lavrov said.
He added that leaving Ukraine's leadership in power would betray those who defeated Nazism in 1945.
The framing collapses on contact with the facts. It was Russia that launched the full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022, and it continues the war today.
Ukraine has no Nazi government. Its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is Jewish and was elected democratically. "Denazification" has functioned since the invasion's first day as a pretext, drawing on the Soviet myth of the Great Patriotic War to recast an attack on Ukrainian identity as a war on fascism.
Earlier, Lavrov said that one of Russia's war goals in Ukraine was to protect the "honor and dignity" of Russian citizens, including their right to use the Russian language and practice the Orthodox faith, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported.
In August, Patriarch Kirill, the leader of the Russian Orthodox Church (ROC), said during a sermon at the Holy Trinity Seraphim-Diveyevo Convent that the Soviet Union's creation of the nuclear bomb was the result of divine intervention.

articles.title: Russia has enough resources to wage war for another 2 years – Ukrainian intelligence agency
articles.body:
Russia has enough resources to wage war for another 2 years – Ukrainian intelligence agency
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has said that Russia has enough resources to continue waging war against Ukraine in 2027 and 2028.
Source: Oleh Ivashchenko, Head of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, in an interview with Ukrinform
Quote: "Meanwhile, it [Russia] still has sufficient resources to wage war against Ukraine. We do not rule out that these resources could last through both 2027 and 2028."
Details: Ivashchenko said that joint efforts with Ukraine's partners are needed to deprive Russia of these resources.
"Sanctions must actually work. We know which countries supply the Russian Federation with electronic components, machine tools and specialised chemicals. Many intermediary companies are emerging that import into Russia goods which subsequently fuel its war machine against us," he said.
Ivashchenko also believes that public discontent among Russians over the war will grow, although it is difficult to say whether this will develop into sufficiently strong protest potential.
"But more than 60% of people are already against the war. This is a consequence of the economic situation and the enemy's heavy personnel losses. We can say that Russia's contract recruitment model has largely exhausted itself. We see that regional budgets in Russia are no longer able to fund payments for contract recruitment. At the same time, Russian troop losses are increasing. Russia's average daily losses range from 1,200 to 1,400 personnel, sometimes reaching 1,500. This includes those killed and seriously wounded," the DIU chief said.
Background: In early June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged Russian leader Vladimir Putin not to continue the war into 2027 and 2028.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: US envoys leave Kyiv without breakthrough on ending war
articles.body:
- 
  US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held “encouraging” talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in their first official visit to Ukraine but made no breakthrough towards ending the war with Russia. The envoys’ trip followed talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday which a Kremlin aide said were “highly useful” while also giving no indication of a breakthrough. Zelenskyy said at a news conference that his talks with the envoys on Sunday covered air defence needs – including Patriot systems – and a “winter package” of support covering both air defence and energy infrastructure before the colder months. He said Kyiv was seeking “serious volumes” of American support on that front, with backing from European partners as well. It appeared the war would continue into winter, he also said.
- 
  Zelenskyy said Russia had intensified strikes on Ukrainian cities before Russia’s State Duma election later this month, calling the attacks deliberate “terror” against civilians. Ukraine was working with 67 domestic companies developing systems to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones at scale. He said the sides agreed to hold a follow-up meeting involving Ukraine, the US and Europe, with a location still to be set.
- 
  The US envoys brought new and “more effective” proposals to Ukraine on ending the war with Russia, according to one senior Ukrainian presidential official. “It’s not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective,” the unnamed offical told Agence France-Presse after the talks with Zelenskyy. “They’re still talking. This is actually the most important part. There are three of them now.” Ukraine’s rail operator announced the envoys’ departure from Kyiv early on Monday.
- 
  Witkoff said earlier that both sides would need to compromise, adding: “We think we have the ingredients to get to that place … and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.” Kushner said: “Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we’ve learned a lot from the trip.”
- 
  In Moscow the US envoys had “discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks”, a White House official said. The Kremlin said the Americans had “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, without elaborating. Witkoff said he was hopeful a new round of US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks would be announced “in short order”. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine while Zelenskyy insists Russia should not be rewarded for its aggression.
- 
  A girl was killed and three other people were wounded in a Ukraine drone attack on the Russia-held Black Sea port city of Sevastopol late on Sunday, the city’s Moscow-appointed governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said on Telegram.
- 
  Russian forces struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel in the Black Sea which was carrying military equipment supplied to the Ukrainian army by western countries, Russian news agencies reported the defence ministry as saying on Sunday.
- 
  Kyiv’s forces struck the Ryazan oil refinery – about 480km (300 miles) inside Russia – causing a fire, Ukraine said on Sunday.
- 
  Russia’s foreign minister said Germany’s accusation that Moscow was involved in a drone incident near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport were, “by and large, the start of a real war”, state news agency Tass reported. “He is, in effect, declaring war on us,” Sergei Lavrov said of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Berlin has ordered a series of measures in response to the attack attempt.

articles.title: Drones Attack Taganrog Airbase
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attacked the military airfield in Taganrog.
This is evidenced by data from NASA’s FIRMS monitoring service.
The attack on the airfield took place overnight on September 6–7, 2026. According to the service’s data, a fire was detected at 2:44 a.m. in the aircraft parking lot.
The airfield is located approximately 40 km from Ukraine’s state border, at coordinates 47.2450, 38.8496.
The Russian military actively uses the airbase. The 325th Aviation Repair Plant (military unit 23213), which specializes in renovating transport aircraft and Il-76 units, is located there.
The Taganrog Aviation Plant shares the airfield with a military unit of the 5th Aviation Group.
Due to the facility’s proximity to Ukraine, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted the plant’s territory and the airfield itself.
South of this airbase is the factory airfield of the PJSC Beriev Aircraft Company.
The facility repairs and upgrades A-50U AEW&C aircraft, Il-76 transport aircraft, and Il-38 patrol aircraft. It also upgrades and services aircraft operated by foreign customers.
In December 2024, the aircraft manufacturing and repair plant was targeted in a combined attack.
At the time, reports indicated that the strike took place at around 4 a.m. Some Russian media outlets claimed that ATACMS ballistic missiles and Palianytsia drone-missiles were used in the attack.
The plant had previously been attacked in March 2024.
Militarnyi previously reported that after a drone threat was declared in Russia’s Rostov region, a fire broke out at the Millerovo airbase, where the 31st Fighter Aviation Regiment, operating Su-30SM aircraft, is based.

articles.title: Russia’s 101st Missile Brigade units deployed in Belarus, equipped with Oreshnik — HUR Chief
articles.body:
Russia’s 101st Missile Brigade units deployed in Belarus, equipped with Oreshnik — HUR Chief
Oleh Ivashchenko, Chief of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR), said this in aninterview with Ukrinform.
He noted that there are currently no signs of Belarus preparing to enter the war against Ukraine, and that the level of military threat to Ukraine from the Belarusian direction is assessed as low.
“However, we are concerned that Belarus has allowed the deployment on its territory of radio-signal repeaters that guide Russian Shahed attack UAVs toward Ukrainian civilian targets and critical infrastructure. We also note the deployment in Belarus of units of the Russian Armed Forces’ 101st Missile Brigade, which is equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range missile system,” Ivashchenko said.
According to Ivashchenko, if Belarus did not grant such permission, this indicates that Minsk no longer controls Russia’s activities on its own territory.

articles.title: Chinese State-Owned Company Supplies Russia With Raw Materials for Geran Drones – Politico
articles.body:
China’s state-owned company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group supplied Russia’s military industry with raw materials used to manufacture attack drones.
The information is based on internal shipping and customs documents obtained by Politico journalists.
The Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation (USCC) collected and analyzed the documents. They have since been verified and shared with the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom. Representatives of the U.S. House Select Committee on China and Ukrainian government officials also independently confirmed the authenticity of the documents.
According to the documents, Jilin Chemical Fiber Group shipped two 40-foot containers containing 46 tons of polyacrylonitrile precursor, a chemical material used in manufacturing, to the Russian company Alabuga-Volokno.
The delivery address listed in the documents belongs to a Rosatom subsidiary located in the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Russia’s Tatarstan region.
The material is a critical precursor in the production of high-strength carbon fiber, which is used in the fabrication of the airframes and internal structural components of Geran loitering munitions. According to estimates, the quantity of precursor material supplied would be sufficient to produce carbon-fiber materials for approximately 1,300 strike UAVs.
To circumvent international export controls, the shipment was declared under a civilian customs classification typically applied to conventional nylon or polyester materials. This classification effectively obscured the transfer of dual-use materials that are subject to international export restrictions.
The Russian company Alabuga-Volokno has been under sanctions imposed by the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and Ukraine since 2023. According to USCC estimates, by 2030, as much as 89% of the company’s total output is expected to be directed toward the needs of Russia’s military industry.
Journalists note that the Chinese manufacturer Jilin Chemical Fiber Group is not currently subject to Western sanctions. USCC analysts have identified at least eight similar tenders for containerized shipments of the material from China to Tatarstan since 2022.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury and Department of State said they take reports of sanctions violations seriously and have the authority to impose additional restrictions on the networks identified in the investigation. The UK Foreign Office has also reviewed the documents provided.
China remains the primary source of critical components for Russia’s defense sector. According to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, China accounts for more than 60% of the imported parts and materials required for the operation of Russia’s military industry.
In return for military assistance, Russia is supplying China with its own technologies to enhance and modernize its defense capabilities.

articles.title: American nuclear attack submarine arrives in Scotland
articles.body:
US Navy submarine spotted arriving at Faslane in Scotland for a routine port visit.
A United States Navy Virginia class attack submarine was spotted running on the surface in the Firth of Clyde on the morning of Monday 7 September.
Sightings of this kind are a familiar part of daily life on both sides of the firth. His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde at Faslane, on the Gare Loch, is the home of the Royal Navy’s submarine service, and the associated armaments depot at Coulport sits on Loch Long a short distance away. Boats entering or leaving the base must pass down the Gare Loch and out through the firth, which brings them within clear view of Dunoon, Gourock, Cloch Point and the surrounding coastline for a considerable stretch of the transit.
The Virginia class is the backbone of the United States Navy’s attack submarine force, a nuclear-powered design built for anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare, land attack with the Tomahawk cruise missile, special operations support and intelligence gathering. Boats of the class have visited the Clyde on a high number of occasions in recent years, and the base is one of a small number of locations in Europe capable of supporting visiting American nuclear submarines alongside.
Surface transits are the norm in these confined and comparatively shallow waters, and the routing takes submarines past some of the most heavily populated coastline in the west of Scotland. As readers will know, that combination has made the Clyde one of the most productive stretches of water in the country for anyone with an interest in naval movements, and community pages in Dunoon, Helensburgh and Inverclyde routinely carry photographs and video of departures and arrivals taken from front windows and hillside paths.
Visits by allied submarines to Faslane are not announced in advance, and neither the Royal Navy nor the United States Navy routinely comments on the movements of individual boats. Port calls of this kind allow for maintenance, stores and crew rest, and they also form part of the wider pattern of American submarine operations in the eastern Atlantic and the waters to the north of Scotland, an area that has drawn steadily greater attention from NATO navies over the past decade.
Movements through the firth are supported by Royal Navy police and Ministry of Defence marine units, and small craft are frequently seen accompanying boats on passage. The waters around the base and the approaches to it are subject to restrictions on the approach of other vessels, and mariners operating in the area are advised of movements through the usual navigational channels.
Work has continued in recent years to expand and modernise the facilities at Faslane under the programme to consolidate the submarine flotilla on the Clyde, covering waterfront infrastructure, engineering support and accommodation, and the base remains one of the largest single employment sites in Scotland.

articles.title: Ukrainian Defense Intelligence Forces Hit Bastion Coastal Missile System in Crimea
articles.body:
Soldiers of the Group 13 unit of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence have hit a Bastion coastal missile system in Crimea.
The agency reported this on social media.
The missile system was hit at the Object 100 site in the area of Biller Ridge.
Group 13 operators also destroyed and hit two fuel trucks and a command-and-staff vehicle belonging to the occupiers on the peninsula.
Previously, during the night of August 16, Ukrainian Navy units struck the same launch positions and the deployment site of the Bastion coastal missile system in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The Bastion system is designed to engage surface ships, but Russia uses it to strike ground targets in Ukraine with P-800 Oniks missiles.
The main threat posed by these anti-ship missiles is their supersonic speed and ability to fly at ultra-low altitudes for up to 300 kilometers, making them difficult targets to intercept.
The system’s self-propelled launcher is based on the MZKT-7930 chassis and is armed with two missiles in transport-launch containers.
In February, the Defense Forces hit the concentration area of Russia’s 15th Separate Coastal Missile Brigade of the Black Sea Fleet in occupied Crimea, which is equipped with Bastion missile systems.
During the night of March 24, Ukrainian units struck Russian military targets, including a Bastion coastal missile system launcher near the settlement of Aktachi in occupied Crimea.
On April 8, Ukrainian forces struck the deployment area of a Bastion coastal missile system near Sofiivka in Crimea.

articles.title: Russia warns US missile system deployment in Norway threatens to reset strategic dialogue to zero
articles.body:
Russia on Monday condemned the US deployment of an advanced missile system to Norway, saying the move dealt a further blow to the prospect of US-Russia talks on strategic nuclear stability.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the deployment in Norway of a missile system based on Mk-41 launchers, which can be used to fire a range of missiles, including Tomahawk cruise missiles, posed a threat because missiles fired from them would be capable of reaching a substantial part of European Russia, including Moscow.
"Steps such as the deployment in Europe of US ground-based intermediate-range missiles that pose a threat to the Russian Federation 'reset to zero' - to put it mildly - the conditions for constructive dialog with the US on strategic issues," the ministry said.
It added that Russia would pay "particular attention" to the deployment sites and command-and-control centers of US missile systems and that they would become targets in the event of a military conflict.
Missile launch system delivered to Norway
US media reports suggested Washington had delivered the new missile launch system to Norway in August.
The Foreign Ministry said dialogue on strategic stability between Moscow and Washington had been curtailed under the previous US administration and described plans by the current administration to pursue multilateral negotiations involving China as "unrealistic."

articles.title: Ukrainian drone blitz hits 3 Russian oil refineries, Zelensky confirms
articles.body:
Ukrainian long-range drones targeted three oil refineries across Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 7.
"Our soldiers continue to respond fairly to Russian strikes on Ukraine. An oil refinery was hit in the Ryazan region. Our long-range force was used against oil refineries in the Perm region and Tatarstan," Zelensky said in a post on social media.
Ukrainian drones also struck a launch and storage site for strike drones in Russia's Kursk Oblast and "a target" in the Black Sea, he added without providing further details, though he did attach a video of highlights.
Zelensky's statement came as Telegram reports, some of which included geolocated details, said that Ukrainian drones struck the LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez refinery, one of Russia's largest oil refineries in Perm, located more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine.
Videos shared by the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ purportedly show Ukrainian long-range drones flying over Perm and smoke rising from the oil refinery amid explosions.
Independent Russian outlet Astra had earlier said on Sept. 6 that Ryazan Oil Refinery Plant, part of Russia's state-controlled oil giant Rosneft, was struck again, following attacks in May and July. With a capacity to process about 17 million tons of oil per year, it produces a wide range of oil products, including automobile gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil, and liquefied gases. The facility is located about 500 kilometers (310 miles) from Ukraine.
Elsewhere in Russia, NASA's FIRMS detected a thermal anomaly at the Taganrog-Central military airfield in Taganrog, near Rostov-on-Don in Rostov Oblast, Militarnyi reported. FIRMS uses satellite instruments to detect thermal anomalies and active fires on Earth's surface. Exilenova+ reported that local residents had reported an attack on Taganrog earlier on Sept. 7.
The Kyiv Independent cannot verify the claims or the extent of the damage caused. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attacks.
Without acknowledging any of the reported attacks, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed on Sept. 7 that it downed or intercepted 306 Ukrainian drones overnight, including over Perm Krai, Rostov Oblast, and Kursk Oblast. It didn't mention Ryazan Oblast in its report. 
The new reported strikesagainst Perm's oil refinery are the latest in a series of attacks that temporarily suspended operations at the site in August. The facility processes more than 13 million metric tons of crude oil annually and produces gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuel, and lubricating oils.
Ukrainian forces had previously struck the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery on July 29 as part of Ukraine's broader missile and drone campaign against Russian energy and oil infrastructure far from Ukraine. 
On Sept. 5, a pro-Ukraine partisan force, Atesh, announced that it had recruited a defector from the Russian military who then destroyed a communications tower near Perm, hindering coordination between security forces in the area. The sabotage reportedly cleared the way for Ukrainian drones to again strike the refinery on Aug. 21. 
In Taganrog, Ukrainian forces previously struck a Russian defense industry facility on April 19. The targeted site was the Atlant-Aero plant, which develops and manufactures strike and reconnaissance drones for the Russian military. A fire broke out at the facility following the strike.

articles.title: Putin backs proposal to allow volunteers with blindness, deafness, schizophrenia, and other severe medical conditions to serve in regional drone-defense units
articles.body:
Putin backs proposal to allow volunteers with blindness, deafness, schizophrenia, and other severe medical conditions to serve in regional drone-defense units
Yevgeny Poddubny, a “war correspondent” for Russian state broadcaster VGTRK who heads United Russia’s electoral list, asked Vladimir Putin to allow volunteers with a Category D fitness classification to serve in regional units defending against Ukrainian drone attacks.
During a medical examination, conscripts and volunteers are assigned one of five fitness categories — A, B, V, G, or D — based on their health. Only people in Categories A and B may be called up for regular conscript service or alternative civilian service.
People in Category V are exempt from regular conscript service and assigned to the reserves. Category G grants a temporary deferment of up to one year, followed by another medical examination. Category D exempts people from military service entirely.
Poddubny claimed that wounded soldiers themselves were asking for the change.
“Of course, people in this category have severe medical conditions, but there are cases where […] people are capable of carrying out certain tasks — for example, serving in regional BARS units for air defense and destroying drones. Obviously, not everyone can. But there is a core group of volunteers who have assessed their own abilities and are pleading for an exception that would allow them to serve in regional units that protect facilities from drones. Obviously, this is not about the front line. Their own city, their own village, their own workplace,” Poddubny said.
Putin replied, “Zhenya, I support it.”
Poddubny made the proposal amid rumors that Russia will see another large-scale wave of mobilization this fall. Russian authorities deny having any such plans. Vladimir Putin has called the mobilization rumors “complete nonsense.”
Category D is assigned to people with severe, irreversible medical conditions, including blindness, deafness in both ears, and schizophrenia.

articles.title: Ukraine Reportedly Hits Russian Ship Carrying Iranian Weapons With 12 Drone Strikes
articles.body:
- Category

Ukraine Reportedly Hits Russian Ship Carrying Iranian Weapons With 12 Drone Strikes
Ukraine reportedly carried out a drone attack against a sanctioned Russian cargo ship in the Mediterranean Sea, striking the vessel 12 times as it allegedly transported Iranian weapons and armored vehicles to Russia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to reports published on September 6, the Russian-flagged Lady Maria was attacked by drones equipped with systems for dropping munitions while sailing in the Mediterranean. Footage circulating online appears to show multiple strikes against the vessel, followed by a fire on board.
Russian opposition journalist Alexander Nevzorov, who published footage of the attack, claimed that Lady Maria sustained 12 direct hits and that the drones were launched from Libyan territory. He also reported that the ship was carrying a shipment of Iranian weapons and armored vehicles from Algeria intended for Russia.
Neither Ukrainian authorities nor other official sources have confirmed Ukraine’s involvement in the attack. The reported contents of the vessel’s cargo and the claim that the drones were launched from Libya have also not been independently verified.
Ship-tracking data showed that Lady Maria, IMO 9220641, had departed the Algerian port of Oran before sailing into the Mediterranean. Recent tracking information placed the vessel near Sicily, while earlier route data indicated that it had passed near Crete in the direction of Syria.
The ship, currently named LADY MARIIA, is under US sanctions and was originally designated under its former name, STELLA-MARIA, due to its connection to Russian shipping company MG-Flot LLC, formerly known as TransMorFlot LLC. Ukraine also sanctioned the vessel on May 23, 2026.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) identifies Lady Maria as a vessel involved in transporting military cargo and weapons for Russia. According to HUR, the ship has operated on the Novorossiysk–Tartus route and has previously been linked to transporting weapons from Syria to Russia.
Earlier, Ukraine reportedly struck another Russian shadow fleet tanker in the Mediterranean, targeting a sanctioned vessel used to transport Russian oil despite Western restrictions.

articles.title: US airman's widow denied benefits as Iran conflict 'not a war'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US military denied widow benefits because Iran conflict 'not a war'
The widow of a US airman killed while taking part in logistical operations during the war on Iran has criticised the US Air Force after she was initially told her husband was not eligible for some combat-related benefits because Washington was not technically “at war”.
Major John Alexander “Alex” Klinner, 33, was one of six US service members killed when a KC-135 refuelling aircraft crashed in western Iraq on 12 March while supporting operations against Iran.
The dispute comes more than six months into the US war with Iran, which has killed at least 18 US service members and wounded 790, according to the Associated Press.
Despite the toll and continuing exchanges of fire, the Trump administration has resisted describing the conflict as a war.
US forces struck targets in Iran twice this week, while Tehran retaliated against US allies in the Gulf as well as tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
Klinner’s widow, Libby Klinner, said the Air Force contacted her this week to clarify that her husband’s final pay did include combat-related hazard pay and tax benefits.
The move came after a social media post in which she said she had previously been told by a military official that her husband was not eligible for some benefits because the United States “was not at war”.
“My husband lost his life because we’re in a war, and then I was told that because it’s not technically a war, we lose out on something,” Klinner told the Associated Press. “It all comes down to principle.”
Her post gained widespread attention in the United States and prompted Vice President JD Vance to promise to look into the case after being questioned about it at a White House briefing.
“We want to be as helpful as we can and ensure she gets everything that she is entitled to,” Vance said.
“My message to her would be, ‘We love ya, we’re grateful for the sacrifice and we very much take very seriously our commitment to get you what you need to get.’”
But when asked separately about the US military campaign against Iran, Vance rejected the term “war”, saying there was “no active shooting”.
His comments came despite the continued exchanges between the two sides, including the US strikes on Iran that week.
President Donald Trump defended Vance’s remarks on Friday, describing the US strikes as “intermittent”.
“I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
The dispute over terminology also comes as Washington has altered the way it records casualties from the confrontation with Iran.
In late July, the Trump administration created a separate category in the Pentagon’s casualty tracking system for those killed and wounded in renewed US-Iran fighting.
Pentagon officials said the change came after “Operation Epic Fury”, the original name for US combat operations against Tehran, had ended.
Since 7 July, all US casualties in the Middle East have instead been recorded under the category “Overseas Operations”.
Klinner said Air Force officials later acknowledged that she had initially been given inaccurate information.
She said officials told her that her husband’s final pay had already included combat-related hazard pay and tax exemptions, but that the payments had been incorrectly itemised, causing confusion.
The Air Force said it had spoken to Klinner to ensure all her questions were addressed and confirmed that all eligible combat-theatre benefits had been included in her husband’s pay.
Combat-related hazard pay is worth $225 a month and does not require a formal declaration of war. Eligibility is instead based on serving in an area where troops face a serious risk of physical injury or hostile fire.

articles.title: China secretly supplied 46 tons of drone-production materials to Russia
articles.body:
The Chinese state-owned Jilin Chemical Fiber Group shipped 46 tons of drone-related chemicals to Russia, disguising the cargo as civilian goods, according to shipping documents reviewed by Politico and The Telegraph.
According to the journalists, the documents named Alabuga-Volokno — a subsidiary of Rosatom — as the recipient of the polyacrylonitrile, a polymer used to produce carbon fiber. Drones based on Iran’s Shahed design have also been assembled since 2023 in Tatarstan’s Alabuga special economic zone.
The documents, dated 2026, list the shipment under a customs code reserved for civilian-use synthetic fiber exports.
David Albright, head of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security, said carbon fiber reinforces a drone’s wings and internal components, including the engine and fuel tank. He estimated the shipment of polyacrylonitrile could produce at least 1,300 drones.
Chinese-made components have long turned up in Russian drones used to strike Ukraine, but the documents mark the first confirmed evidence of direct material supplies from China, Politico said.
The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center (USCC) obtained the documents detailing chemical shipments from China. The Ukrainian government and a special U.S. House of Representatives committee on China confirmed the documents’ authenticity, Politico’s sources said. The documents were also shared with the British government for review.

articles.title: Some ten robot boats. Five hundred Russian air sorties. One very lopsided hunt
articles.body:
Russia flew hundreds of warplane sorties against a small group of Ukrainian sea drones, according to the ArmyInform. The drones belong to Group 13, a Ukrainian military-intelligence unit. The unit is running out of Russian warships to sink and now strikes land targets from the sea, its commander, known by his call sign Thirteenth, said.
Years ago, Russia entered its all-out war against Ukraine with a commanding navy and treated the Black Sea as its own. A country left with almost no warships has since answered with cheap robot boats, turning expendable machines into the tool that now contests that sea.
More than 500 sorties to hunt one small drone group
Group 13 hunts Russian warships with Magura sea drones—uncrewed attack boats. Russia flew more than 500 aircraft sorties against a group of eight to 10 Magura drones at the time, the commander said. Moscow spent more on locating the drones than the unit's entire mission cost, he added. Missions have grown longer, too. What once took a day now takes three, four, or five days.
Biggest Magura sea drone doesn’t ram ships. It carries other drones and stays out seven days
The commander split the unit's rise into three stages: victory at sea, an end to Russian air dominance over the water, and now strikes on land from the sea. The bar set in 2023 and 2024 is unrealistic to hold in the Black Sea today, he said, because there are no ship targets left, and what remains is harder to reach. A struck S-400 air-defense system does not pay off like a sunk warship, he added.
The bill for Russia
The damage runs past destroyed hardware. Each Russian sailor killed leaves a family pension to pay and training to write off, the commander said. He pointed to the Syrian Express, Russia's sea supply line to Syria. It once ran a short route and now goes through the Baltic Sea, and the whole bill runs into the millions, he said.
The unit's capabilities came together in a strike on the Ivan Khurs, a Russian reconnaissance ship, its first target. The later sinking of the missile boat Ivanovets killed 40 Russian crew in minutes, the commander recalled. He expects the unit to be remembered as revolutionaries, likening its sea drones to the first tanks more than a century ago.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of air raids, missile strikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of air raids, missile strikes
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Monday accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out airstrikes around the country as the rebels press a deadly offensive to seize territory bordering the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.
The attacks targeted Houthi positions around the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country, which is divided between areas held by the rebels and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.
"The Saudi enemy targeted the provinces of Jawf, al-Bayda, Marib and Taiz with several airstrikes and cruise missiles," said the Saba news agency, which is affiliated with the Houthi movement.
Days of fighting near the Red Sea coast has left more than 300 people dead and displaced hundreds of families as the Houthis try to capture land bordering the Bab al-Mandab.
The narrow waterway forms the southern entrance to the Red Sea, a shipping artery that has become a vital route for Saudi oil exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, the gateway to the Gulf, during the US-Iran war.
AFP news agency, citing military sources within the government forces, reported the air raids and missile attacks. They have not been claimed by Saudi Arabia.
Most of the strikes were in Al Bayda and Marib, aiming at strategic positions, gatherings, and camps under Houthi control, the sources said on condition of anonymity.
On Saturday, AFP reported- citing a military official- that Saudi airstrikes had targeted positions recently seized by the Houthis in Taiz governorate.
The Houthis and government forces have been fighting for days over control of the Bab al-Mandab, the deadliest flare-up in Yemen since a 2022 ceasefire collapsed in July.
The Houthis, whose attacks seriously disrupted Red Sea shipping during the Gaza war, have also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and have been targeting its ships and territory.

articles.title: Ukraine lost over US$1 billion on defence procurement in one year – NYT
articles.body:
Ukraine lost over US$1 billion on defence procurement in one year – NYT
Ukraine lost around US$1.2 billion in 2024 alone due to fraud, waste and mismanagement in defence procurement. Meanwhile, the country continued to award contracts to unreliable suppliers.
Source: The New York Times, citing classified findings from government audits for 2024 and 2025
Details: The newspaper examined three striking examples of defence procurement fraud identified in the audit reports.
In 2024, the Pavlohrad Chemical Plant supplied the military with thousands of defective mortar shells. Its director, Leonid Shyman, was eventually arrested in one of the most high-profile cases of alleged fraud in Ukraine's wartime defence industry.
However, even after it became clear that the shells were defective, government audit findings show that the Defence Procurement Agency (DPA) continued to award new contracts to Shyman.
For example, the government awarded a US$280 million contract while he was out on bail on corruption charges.
Overall, seven of Ukraine's 10 largest arms manufacturers received new contracts despite ongoing criminal investigations into fraud, failures to fulfil previous contracts or the arrests of executives on corruption charges.
Audit documents indicate that warning signs in procurement were disregarded and that overcharging or failures to fulfil delivery obligations rarely resulted in consequences.
Some companies were also awarded contracts without demonstrating that they were capable of supplying the weapons or without holding the necessary licences to do so. Auditors identified 18 companies that were awarded deals despite failing to fulfil previous contracts. Six of them had not successfully completed a single contract.
Around US$126 million was lost as a result of lower bids being disregarded and weapons being purchased at inflated prices. Auditors said the contracts had been awarded without a legal basis.
Second example
Another case involved a 2024 DPA tender to purchase rocket artillery ammunition worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Three companies submitted bids. The first said it could supply the rockets for the equivalent of about US$4,200 each. Another asked for US$4,600 per rocket, while the third quoted US$5,100.
All of the rockets were identical – manufactured at the same factory by the same company in Türkiye – and the only difference was the price. The Turkish manufacturer, Arca Defense, offered the lowest price through a direct sale from its factory.
However, the contract was awarded to the company that submitted the highest bid – a subsidiary of the Czechoslovak Group, a major Czech holding company. Rather than buying directly from the manufacturer, the government paid the Czech company to act as an intermediary.
The decision added around US$130 million to Ukraine's bill for the rockets. The reports said auditors found no justification for the decision.
Despite the auditors' concerns, Ukraine considered another deal with the company, this time to replace its stock of Kalashnikov rifles with a Czech-designed NATO-calibre model. No agreement has been reported as having been concluded.
Third example
Also in 2024, the DPA sought to purchase Soviet-designed rockets from a Serbian manufacturer. Given Serbia's pro-Russian policies, Ukraine used a chain of intermediaries to obtain the rockets.
The government awarded the contract to Spetstechnoexport, a Ukrainian state-owned arms intermediary with a history of failing to fulfil contracts.
Spetstechnoexport also lacked a Serbian export licence for the rockets. Instead, the company provided a "letter of guarantee" from Ukraine's Defence Intelligence, auditors found.
The company then subcontracted the deal to US arms company Regulus. Rustem Umierov, Ukraine's defence minister at the time, wanted to remove intermediaries from Ukraine's wartime arms procurement.
He asked Regulus to negotiate directly with the state procurement agency, effectively cutting Spetstechnoexport out of the deal. The agreement subsequently fell through.
As a result, the Ukrainian government sued Spetstechnoexport to recover late-payment penalties and interest. Spetstechnoexport, in turn, sought money from Regulus.
Background: In May, the DPA contracted a record quantity of long-range 155mm artillery rounds, with competition helping to save 16% of the initial amount.

articles.title: Ukraine lost $1.2 bn to defense fraud and waste in one year – NYT
articles.body:
Ukraine lost $1.2 bn to defense fraud and waste in one year – NYT
Ukraine lost around $1.2 billion to fraud, waste and mismanagement in military procurement in 2024 alone, the New York Times has reported, citing confidential government audits and court records.
Seven of the country’s ten largest military contractors continued to receive new orders despite fraud investigations, previous failures to deliver, or the arrest of executives on corruption charges, the paper wrote on Sunday, describing the pattern as a “persistent phenomenon.”
Auditors also identified 18 companies awarded contracts despite earlier defaults, six of which had failed to fulfill a single deal.
Defense industry fraud is “a longstanding tradition” in Ukraine, American anti-corruption expert James Wasserstrom has told the NYT. “Anything that isn’t nailed down in Ukraine will be stolen,” he said.
Among the cases highlighted by the Times was the state-owned Pavlohrad Chemical Plant, which supplied the military with 233,000 unusable mortar rounds. Nevertheless, the company later received more business, including a contract to supply nearly all of Ukraine’s 122mm artillery rounds in 2025.
The audits also found that cheaper offers were sometimes bypassed. In one tender, Kiev reportedly bought Turkish-made munitions for multiple-launch rocket systems through a Czech intermediary for around $5,100 each despite the manufacturer offering them directly for roughly $4,200.
The losses accumulated as Vladimir Zelensky repeatedly appealed to Western governments for more weapons, warning of critical shortages on the battlefield. In April 2024, he said Kiev was in “dire need” of increased support and pressed its backers to deliver promised arms and ammunition.
The report comes amid a series of high-profile graft investigations involving top Ukrainian officials and figures close to Zelensky. In August, the Ukrainian leader sacked the deputy head of his office, Irina Mudraya, while other recent corruption probes have implicated former ministers, diplomats and senior officials.
Former Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov, meanwhile, accused the government of “systemic corruption” following his dismissal in July. Fedorov, who had sought to overhaul military procurement, has claimed that entrenched defense-industry interests resisted his reforms and has since called for wartime elections.
Zelensky’s five-year presidential term expired in May 2024, but he has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law imposed after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022.
Moscow has long argued that the scandals are evidence of systemic corruption in Ukraine. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said earlier this year that corruption “permeates the entire Ukrainian power structure, including Zelensky’s inner circle and Zelensky himself.”

articles.title: L3Harris finishes first F-16 shield systems for allies
articles.body:
- L3Harris completed the first 35 Viper Shield electronic warfare systems for F-16 jets, with eight allied nations now ordering 233 units total.
- The $1 billion program, funded by foreign partners including Peru, Poland and Taiwan, could let the U.S. Air Force join later without paying upfront development costs.
L3Harris Technologies has finished building the first 35 units of an electronic warfare system designed to protect F-16 fighter jets from radar-guided missiles and other threats, the company announced, marking the start of full production after years of development.
The system, called Viper Shield and officially designated the AN/ALQ-254(V)1, detects and jams enemy radar signals to help F-16 pilots avoid being tracked or hit. L3Harris builds it in two forms: mounted inside the aircraft or carried as an external pod, and the company said it also assembled its first pod using the same production line. Eight allied nations have now ordered the system, and L3Harris is ramping up toward full-rate production to fill a combined order of 233 units.
Lockheed Martin and the U.S. Air Force selected L3Harris in 2021 to build Viper Shield specifically for the newest version of the F-16, the Block 70/72, which Lockheed sells primarily to foreign buyers rather than the U.S. military. The system pairs a digital radar warning receiver with a jamming technique known as digital radio frequency memory, which can mimic and confuse enemy radar signals, and it’s built to work with the F-16’s newer APG-83 radar as well as older F-16 models already in service.
Confirmed Viper Shield customers include Bahrain, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Morocco, Taiwan and Poland, along with Peru, which selected the system in August for a fleet of 12 new F-16 Block 70 jets that will replace its aging Mirage 2000s and Russian-made MiG-29s. L3Harris has not named the eighth country in the program.
“The $1 billion shared investment by countries operating F-16s means the U.S. Air Force and National Guard could benefit from joining the program,” said Chris Aebli, president of Communications & Spectrum Dominance at L3Harris. “The foreign investment is funding development, lab testing, flight testing and current production of Viper Shield systems, which presents the United States with a savings opportunity to avoid upfront costs.”
That $1 billion figure reflects the combined value of orders placed by the eight partner nations so far, and L3Harris has said it’s in discussions with additional countries that could add another $1.5 billion in demand. Because those foreign orders are already funding the system’s development and manufacturing line, the U.S. Air Force could potentially adopt Viper Shield later without covering the upfront research and testing costs itself, something L3Harris has pointed to as a selling point for eventual American use.

Russia slams US despatch of missile system to Norway as another blow to idea of arms talks
MOSCOW, Sept 7 - Russia on Monday condemned the U.S. deployment of an advanced missile system to Norway, saying the move dealt a further blow to the prospect of U.S.-Russia talks on strategic nuclear stability.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the deployment in Norway of a missile system based on Mk-41 launchers which can be used to fire a range of missiles, includingTomahawk cruise missiles, posed a threat because missiles fired from them would be capable of reaching a substantial part of European Russia, including Moscow.
"Steps such as the deployment in Europe of U.S. ground-based intermediate range missiles that pose a threat to the Russian Federation 'reset to zero' - to put it mildly - the conditions for constructive dialogue with the US on strategic issues," the ministry said.
It added that Russia would pay "particular attention" to the deployment sites and command-and-control centres of U.S. missile systems and that they would become targets in the event of a military conflict.
U.S. media reports suggested Washington had delivered the new missile launch system to Norway in August.
