Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova Monday said the deployment of US missile systems in Norway was another “highly destabilizing” move by NATO and accused the alliance of seeking to expand its capability to launch missile strikes deep into Russian territory.
“We regard the deployment in Europe of US systems capable of launching intermediate- and shorter-range missiles as yet another step in the never-ending series of highly destabilizing actions by NATO countries,” Zakharova said.
She accused NATO of seeking to establish control over key maritime routes in the region, saying the US systems deployed in Norway are based on Mk-41 launch cells capable of firing missiles against targets on land and at sea.
She said the systems can launch long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles and that their deployment in Norway puts a significant portion of European Russia, including Moscow, within range.
“Thus, these missile systems can be used in aggressive actions by NATO countries against our country to solve strategic problems,” she said.
The spokeswoman warned that the US missile systems and their command and support infrastructure in Norway would become a focus of Russia’s strategic deterrence forces, including planning for the use of strike capabilities in the event of an armed conflict.
Regarding strategic stability talks with the US, Zakharova said the dialogue had not stalled but was “unilaterally interrupted” by the administration of former President Joe Biden.
She criticized the current US administration’s calls for multilateral negotiations involving China, saying Beijing had repeatedly made clear it had strong reasons not to participate at this stage.
Zakharova said conditions for substantive and productive strategic stability talks between Moscow and Washington had not been established.
“Steps such as the deployment in Europe of US ground-based intermediate- and shorter-range missile systems that threaten Russia will, to put it mildly, ‘zero out’ the prerequisites for constructive talks with the US on strategic issues,” she said.

articles.title: Russian journalists fled their country after the invasion of Ukraine. My Undesirable Friends: Part II follows their lives in exile.
articles.body:
Russian journalists fled their country after the invasion of Ukraine. My Undesirable Friends: Part II follows their lives in exile.
The Venice Film Festival hosted the world premiere of My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile, a documentary by Russian-born American filmmaker Julia Loktev. The film follows journalists from TV Rain, iStories, and Novaya Gazeta as they find themselves in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In this latest chapter of her documentary epic about Russian journalists, Loktev explores how her subjects struggle to find their footing and keep doing their work despite the challenges of life abroad. Film critic Anton Dolin reviews the film for Meduza.
An unwitting déjà vu. With a flicker of dread, you realize you’re about to sit through six hours of documentary footage on a subject you’ve already studied in exhaustive detail — and lived through yourself. Then the film draws you in: you start worrying about the people on screen and can’t tear yourself away. By the end, your head is full of thoughts you want to share with readers and future viewers alike — until you remember that a year and a half ago, you already wrote about Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends.
I flip through that piece, nodding along, and find myself agreeing with what I wrote. The important things have already been said. What is there to add? Do I really need to retell the “plot” that pushes the film’s characters — journalists from TV Rain, iStories, and Novaya Gazeta — into forced emigration and scatters the action across a dozen locations?
At the time, I wrote that I was watching Loktev’s nonfiction epic as my own story. That’s not exaggeration: you’re reading this piece by a film critic convicted in absentia and designated a foreign agent by Russian authorities, writing for a publication that Russia has declared an “undesirable organization.”
What’s more interesting is something else. Over more than a year in theaters, My Undesirable Friends has found viewers across a striking range of countries — from Iran to the United States, from Belarus to Israel — who recognize themselves in this unusual film, an iPhone-shot chronicle of shattered hopes seen through the eyes of young Russian liberal journalists.
Unconventional in every respect, the film has landed on numerous “best of the year” lists, won best documentary at the Gotham Independent Film Awards, and made the Oscar shortlist. Loktev seems to have captured the spirit of the times — the “last air” referenced in the subtitle of the first part of My Undesirable Friends.
At roughly 12 hours total, the project invites comparisons to a great Russian novel — or any novel of similar sprawl — whose sheer volume is at once intimidating and comforting. A simpler analogy is a TV series: My Undesirable Friends is divided into 10 chapters, and that’s no accident.
But watching it in a theater matters. The deliberate clash between the homemade, chronicle-like iPhone footage and the sheer scale of the runtime and the screen captures an essential paradox: the tragic, almost grotesque imbalance between the smallness of a person under political persecution and the unencompassable scale of the historical machine that grinds any one of us to dust.
There’s something else, too. You don’t step into the theater to unwind — you’re condemned, in effect, to live there for a while, growing close to characters who mature and change before your eyes. A cold, detached gaze is almost impossible. The film demands your empathy. By the end, these “undesirables” become your friends, too.
Loktev, absent from the frame, shoots and edits without hurry, without compressing time, letting air into other people’s claustrophobic spaces — perhaps not the last air after all, since everyone ultimately manages to escape and survive. Her touch is delicate enough to reveal her as more than a sympathizer. As Novaya Gazeta put it, she’s an accomplice.
It’s not only a TV series or a novel that can stretch across long, endless hours — life does too. When you’re caught in the thick of events, especially shocking and dramatic ones, you lose the ability to see them from a distance. Film has that resource. By giving shape to the formlessness of reality, My Undesirable Friends reveals patterns and, carefully, step by step, leads its lost, hapless émigrés toward the light — maybe not toward the triumph of good over evil, but at least toward clarity.
The credits seem to separate “characters” from “performers.” The former are listed by diminutive first names, without surnames — they’re friends, after all. The latter are real people. Who is playing whom? Playing, or, on the contrary, shedding a social mask and setting aside a professional role to let real emotion through?
In the film’s first chapter, set in spring 2022, Anya — Anna Nemzer — is in Israel, bewildered, preparing to leave for Georgia. Ksyusha (Ksenia Mironova) and Lera (Valeria Ratnikova) are in tears, trying to check into a random hotel in Istanbul. Alesya (Alesya Marokhovskaya) and Ira (Irina Dolinina) look around uncertainly in Prague. And Lena (Elena Kostyuchenko), her voice full of horror, states the inevitable: to file truthful reports from Ukraine, she’ll have to quit Novaya Gazeta.
By the end, each character’s arc feels complete, even though all of them — young, full of energy and even hope — remain at a crossroads on their own path, far from any imagined destination. The film does have one unqualified advantage over life: it gets to end with closing credits.
The Venice Film Festival, where Part II of My Undesirable Friends is having its world premiere, is hosting several other monumental documentaries this year: Sergei Loznitsa’s three-hour Imperium, Alex Gibney’s four-hour Musk, and Mariano Llinás’s five-hour Life of Jorge Luis Borges. Loktev’s runtime sets a record even against that field — and this is only half the entire film. Apparently only films this uncompromisingly detailed, this painstakingly thorough, can answer the unasked questions of a disoriented viewer.
A brief digression: this summer’s most unconventional box-office hit was Christopher Nolan’s three-hour The Odyssey, whose sheer length did nothing to deter audiences. The characters of My Undesirable Friends wander uncharted seas and hostile islands while their own Trojan War rages on. They don’t have a single chance yet to sail off into the sunset.
Loktev’s film, though, moves past the two basic plots in Borges’s classification cited above: it isn’t a siege story (that was Last Air in Moscow), and it isn’t a homecoming that can only be dreamed of. The third Borgesian plot is the search. Ksyusha, Lera and Anya, Lena, Alesya and Ira are searching not just for a safe harbor but for the lost meaning of their work — and, with it, of their existence. Loktev, stitching scattered misadventures into a patchwork of a unified narrative, helps them find that meaning, but does so, fortunately, without moralizing or drawing categorical conclusions.
Tel Aviv and Riga, Tbilisi and Amsterdam, New York and Prague, Istanbul and Washington, and finally — how could they not appear? — Moscow and Kyiv… Ksyusha, stone-faced, walks out of the courthouse where her fiancé, Ivan Safronov, was sentenced to 22 years in prison. Lera fantasizes about The Hague, where she imagines herself reporting live on air during Putin’s trial. Anya discusses the news with her father over Zoom, then tries to locate the spot in her body that reacts to the sale of her grandmother’s apartment — somewhere near the solar plexus.
Meanwhile, Lena and her girlfriend, Yana (Yana Kuchina), seriously discuss Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB)‘s plans to kill Lena, then, just to be sure, tell their fortune with a book — a random volume of Harry Potter that happened to be at hand. Rowling’s grim fairy tale also appeared in the first part of the film. It’s easier to imagine yourself fighting dementors and death eaters if you’re still hoping for a happy ending.
Warning: this video contains explicit language.
The climax arrives in the fourth, penultimate chapter. While Lena works on a book with the provocative title Moya Lyubimaya Strana — “My Favorite Country” (in the Russian edition, the word “favorite” is censored with asterisks, leaving readers plenty of room for interpretation) — TV Rain lands at the center of a scandal in Latvia, where opposition television journalists who had fled Russia had obtained a broadcasting license. Twice, they let the phrase “our army,” referring to the Russian army, go out on air. For that, they would lose their right to work and their visas — exiled once again.
Loktev tells this story from start to finish, without omissions, foregrounding the internal and external chaos of everyone caught up in the conflict. A single possessive pronoun becomes the apple of discord. There’s no room for compromise. The two sides in the standoff speak different languages — and no, not Latvian and Russian. The rift runs far deeper than a linguistic misunderstanding.
Surprisingly, it’s this episode that dots the i’s. The resolution itself is ambivalent: in the moment, Latvian authorities win, while a later court ruling overturns the fairness of their decision. But more than two years have passed since then, and TV Rain relocated to the Netherlands long ago, where it now broadcasts — probably for the best, for everyone involved.
It’s exactly then, in the winter of 2022–2023, that it becomes clear opposition journalists from Russia no longer have an “ours” on either side of the border. But that also means their moral choices are made without regard for “their own.” At this point My Undesirable Friends — “my,” another possessive — finally takes shape as a film about choice and the act of claiming agency. This is what the characters were searching for all along: not a home, not a job, not stability, but an inner anchor that would let them keep doing their work, whatever stood in the way.
Navalny’s killing — Lera cries reading the news at her monitor. Trump’s inauguration — Ksyusha, in Washington, finds herself in the middle of the celebrations. This story has no ending and can’t have one. Sometimes, it turns out, you don’t need a resolution — a setup is enough. New characters appear: former TV Rain journalist Petya (Peter Ruzavin) and his Ukrainian wife, Natalka (Natalia Humeniuk, the former head of the Ukrainian news outlet Hromadske). Blurring the increasingly faint line between journalism and activism, they find support in each other. However irresponsible their dreams for the future may be, the path they’ve chosen is perfectly clear. Petya goes off to fight for Ukraine, and his personal story opens a new chapter.
For all its chronicle-like quality and seeming neutrality, My Undesirable Friends restores, as if by a wave of a magic wand, faith in the idea that everyone has power over their own tomorrow — even if the day after tomorrow is shrouded in impenetrable fog. It’s probably an illusion, but the kind of illusion that, even in the worst of times, makes life feel meaningful.

articles.title: IAEA has been completely blind to Iran’s nuclear program for over a year, Rafael Grossi says
articles.body:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is completely blind regarding Iran's nuclear program and has been since at least June 2025, the agency's Director-General Rafael Grossi told its Board of Governors on Monday.
Grossi said, "As stated in the report...the Agency has neither received information from Iran regarding the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities nor had access to any of those facilities to conduct in-field verification activities. Therefore, the Agency was unable to discharge its safeguards responsibilities under the NPT Safeguards Agreement at declared nuclear facilities in Iran.
"Consequently, we were not able to verify their status for safeguards purposes and the associated nuclear material, and as a result I am also unable to report in relation to the implementation by Iran of relevant provisions of the UN Security Council resolutions or the Board’s resolutions of November last year and June this year," he continued.
Further, he said, "It is more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge in relation to the previously declared inventories of LEU and HEU enriched up to 60% U-235 at the declared nuclear facilities affected by the military attacks of June 2025," referring to Israel's war with Iran last year.
Next, he noted, "The Agency’s lack of information about these facilities and associated nuclear material and our inability to conduct verification activities at these facilities is a matter of serious proliferation concern. The situation needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency."
Moreover, Grossi said, he called on Iran "to engage with the Agency constructively in order to make possible the full and effective implementation of Agency safeguards in Iran and to fulfill its responsibilities under the NPT Safeguards Agreement.
"A return to diplomacy and negotiations aimed at finding a solution to issues related to Iran’s nuclear program is imperative, and the Agency stands ready to support such efforts. The situation regarding Iran’s nuclear program has implications for the global non-proliferation regime," he warned.
Iran refuses access to IAEA inspectors since joint Israel-US attacks
Since Israel and the US struck Iran in June 2025, Tehran has refused access to the IAEA to any of its nuclear facilities, claiming that the agency would pass on classified information to those who attacked it.
While Grossi at points has said that solving nuclear issues by the use of force is less productive than diplomacy, the Islamic regime has viewed his stance on American and Israeli attacks on Iran's nuclear program in 2025-2026 as too mild, and taken offense that he has not condemned the attacks more forcefully.
However, while Grossi has complained that Iran has cut off IAEA access almost completely in 2025-2026 - with the exception of a visit to the Bushehr nuclear facility, which has never presented any threat - in fact, the Islamic Republic started to significantly limit IAEA inspector access as early as 2021.
As early as November 2021, Grossi cited the Islamic Republic's violation of a supposed deal from September 12, 2021, to renew IAEA access to the critical Karaj nuclear site. Because Tehran reneged on the deal, Grossi said, "the lack of access to the Karaj workshop has meant that the restoration of surveillance and monitoring at all of Iran’s facilities and locations in relation to the JCPOA could not be completed. This is seriously affecting the Agency’s ability to restore continuity of knowledge at the workshop, which has been widely recognized as essential in relation to a return to the JCPOA" 2015 nuclear deal.
Iran’s IAEA obstruction predates the 2025 war with Israel
Going back further in time, Iran has accused the US of being the first to violate the 2015 deal when first-term US President Donald Trump pulled out of that deal in May 2018.
However, when Trump pulled out, he noted that the Mossad had provided tens of thousands of files of evidence of Iranian lying and cheating relating to the deal when it seized Iran's nuclear archives in January 2018.
Although Iran was certainly complying with some significant aspects of the deal, the archives proved that the regime was also systematically seeking to hide the weapons aspects of the nuclear program from the IAEA and the West.
Currently, neither Iran nor the US is pushing for IAEA involvement until they resolve their other ongoing standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
Israel remains concerned that whatever is left of Iran's nuclear program after the 2025-2026 strikes has not yet been closed down as is not being overseen by IAEA inspectors.

articles.title: Greece wants deeper ties with both Israel and Arab countries
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Greece wants deeper ties with both Israel and Arab countries
Greece will press ahead with its strategic defence cooperation with Israel but also wants to deepen relations with other states in the Middle East, Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Sunday.
Greece-Israeli ties and defence, security and energy cooperation have grown closer over the past decade, and Mitsotakis enjoys a friendly rapport with his counterpart, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Shared concerns about Turkey have helped boost ties. The two countries signed a 3-billion-euro ($3.5 billion) deal on 31 August for Israel to build an air defence shield in Greece.
Mitsotakis told reporters in Thessaloniki that Greece is one of only five NATO countries spending at least 3.5 percent of its GDP on core defence.
Greece’s traditionally high spending has been fueled by almost constant tensions with Turkey, and its questioning of Greek sovereignty over parts of the Aegean Sea and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Greece recognises only the demarcation of the two countries’ respective maritime zones as an issue to be negotiated or sent to international arbitration.
Asked about US President Donald Trump’s expressed desire to sell the advanced F-35 multirole combat aircraft to Turkey, Mitsotakis replied that he will not tell the US what to do, but noted that legal obstacles remain as Turkey was sanctioned for buying the S-400 air defence system from Russia.
Greece will take delivery of its first 20 F-35s in late 2028, with an option to buy 20 more.
Mitsotakis also said he planned to visit Saudi Arabia soon, and that the recently concluded Mecca Joint Defence Agreement among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey changes nothing in Greece’s relations with Riyadh.
Greece has maintained an air defence battery in Saudi Arabia since 2021, and has used its Patriot missiles four times since July to down drones and ballistic missiles, allegedly from Yemen, aimed at the kingdom’s oil refineries.

articles.title: The economic risks of a Gulf tanker war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
As Gulf crisis morphs to tanker war, what economic implications?
The escalating conflict in the Strait of Hormuz is beginning to pose a much bigger question for Gulf economies: how long can their enormous financial reserves shield them from a prolonged disruption to one of the world's most important energy routes?
For now, countries including the UAE, Qatar and Kuwait have formidable financial defences. But analysts warn that even those buffers have limits if the crisis stretches into 2027.
Fitch Ratings has warned that “rating risks for some issuers in Gulf Cooperation Council countries could increase under a hypothetical scenario in which passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted through most of 2027”.
The agency said the “extremely large sovereign financial buffers in Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar have been a key factor in limiting the conflict’s impact on credit ratings”. But the longer the disruption continues, the more those reserves risk being drawn down to compensate for falling exports, higher shipping and insurance costs, and wider economic damage.
Firas Shaabo, professor of financial management at Istanbul’s Başakşehir University, says the immediate problem is not whether Gulf states have enough money. It is the accumulating “cost of the shock”.
Sovereign wealth funds give governments considerable room to absorb the impact, he says, but that protection is temporary rather than unlimited.
The warning comes as the confrontation at sea has sharply intensified. US Central Command announced that it had targeted three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard launched ballistic missiles towards two US warships.
The IRGC subsequently said it had targeted three tankers which, according to its account, were travelling along unauthorised routes through Hormuz, as well as three vessels linked to the United States.
The result is a rapidly deteriorating environment for shipping, insurance and trade finance - and Gulf economies are among the most exposed. Two large tankers carrying Saudi crude were attacked almost simultaneously as they left the Strait of Hormuz on 31 August.
The Saudi tanker Sadr and the Liberia-flagged Senegal Prosperity were each carrying about two million barrels of crude. Saudi Arabia's National Shipping Company, Bahri, later said two Filipino crew members aboard the Sadr had been killed.
By 2 September, the International Maritime Organization had recorded 72 confirmed incidents targeting international shipping in the region, with 21 seafarers killed.
Shipping slows to a trickle
The scale of the disruption can already be seen in vessel movements. Kpler data showed only five commercial ships passing through Hormuz last Saturday. None were recorded crossing on Sunday.
That compared with 31 vessels during the previous weekend. Traffic remained in single digits at the beginning of September, as large oil and gas carriers increasingly avoided the strait.
For Gulf exporters, that matters because Hormuz is not simply a shipping route. For several states, it is the principal outlet through which their energy exports reach international markets.
Saudi Arabia has some ability to bypass it through infrastructure connecting its oil industry to the Red Sea. Other Gulf states have far fewer alternatives.
Fitch said financial reserves would continue to provide substantial protection under a prolonged-conflict scenario, but warned that extended disruption could eventually damage the credit profiles of states without alternative export routes such as pipelines bypassing Hormuz.
The effect is being amplified by extraordinary increases in insurance costs. War-risk premiums for crude tankers have risen from about 0.25% of a vessel's value before the confrontation to between 7.5% and 12.5% in August.
For shipowners, that can make voyages commercially unattractive. Operators must either absorb enormous additional costs, pass them on through higher freight rates or avoid the region altogether.
When large reserves are not enough
The Gulf states are often portrayed as possessing almost inexhaustible financial resources because of the size of their sovereign wealth funds. But Shaabo says that can be misleading.
Those funds are not vast pools of cash that governments can immediately deploy. Their holdings range from relatively small amounts of liquid reserves, to investments that can be sold quickly but potentially at a loss during turbulent markets, and large portfolios of long-term assets that cannot easily be converted into cash.
The important question, therefore, is not simply how large a country's sovereign wealth fund is. It is how much immediately accessible liquidity it has - and how long that liquidity can sustain government spending and economic support if the disruption continues.
That distinction becomes increasingly important if the Hormuz crisis moves from a temporary shock to a persistent economic problem. A prolonged disruption could weaken growth and government revenues at the same time as states face higher spending requirements.
Eventually, Shaabo warns, that combination could begin affecting sovereign creditworthiness.
Higher oil prices offer only partial protection. They may increase the value of every barrel Gulf producers are able to export, helping compensate for some losses.
But higher prices matter much less if exporters cannot physically move the same quantities of crude. Restricted export routes mean lower volumes, while transport, insurance and import costs rise sharply.
The result could be weaker economic activity even as headline oil prices remain high.
Iran has added to that uncertainty by expanding the number of vessels on its blacklist in the strait to 56 on 2 September. The list includes oil tankers and carriers of liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas.
Iran has threatened listed vessels with fines, seizure or detention, and warned that action could also be taken against ships conducting ship-to-ship cargo transfers with them, according to Reuters.
A crisis extending beyond oil
The risks are also spreading into the financial and legal machinery underpinning international trade. The continuing turmoil has exposed weaknesses in insurance contracts used by lenders and charterers to finance shipments.
Some war-risk clauses may not have been designed for a crisis developing at the current pace. That creates uncertainty over who carries the financial risk when vessels are prevented from sailing or when routes suddenly become too dangerous.
Ship charter agreements can also limit an owner's ability to avoid areas formally designated as war-risk zones. According to Lloyd's List, the result could be prolonged contractual disputes, higher litigation costs and reduced availability of trade finance.
That means the impact of the Hormuz confrontation does not stop with oil tankers. It can gradually spread through banks, insurers, shipping companies, importers and government finances.
Three possible paths
Shaabo sees three broad scenarios. The first - and in his view currently the least likely - is a relatively rapid settlement followed by the gradual resumption of shipping.
Under that scenario, Gulf governments could rely on reserves, additional borrowing and adjustments to spending without putting their sovereign ratings under serious pressure.
The second is considerably more damaging. If disruption lasts several months, what begins as a shipping and logistics crisis could develop into a wider financial and economic problem.
Growth could slow as inflation and government spending rise. Capital could leave the region, bank profits could decline and major investments in transport, logistics, tourism and property could be delayed.
Governments would then face an increasingly difficult choice between maintaining spending and subsidies, depleting financial assets or taking on substantially more debt.
The third scenario is the most severe. Shaabo estimates a 20% to 25% probability of sustained physical damage to infrastructure including oil facilities, ports, refineries, pipelines and power stations.
At that point, the nature of the crisis changes. It would no longer simply be a question of temporarily preventing Gulf states from exporting what they produce.
Their ability to produce energy itself could be reduced. Sovereign wealth funds are far less effective against that kind of shock because the problem becomes a loss of future income rather than a temporary shortage of cash.
That could lead directly to negative reviews of sovereign credit ratings.
Not all Gulf states face the same risk
The impact would also be highly uneven. Economic expert and financial adviser Ali Ahmed Darwish says the Fitch warning should be treated with particular seriousness because the crisis highlights significant differences between Gulf economies.
Saudi Arabia has the advantage of alternative export infrastructure towards the Red Sea. For states whose geography leaves them overwhelmingly dependent on Hormuz, the options are much narrower.
Those countries may eventually have to undertake far-reaching changes to their supply and export networks. But alternative routes can be extremely expensive, technically difficult or simply impractical.
Darwish argues that governments will therefore also need to make greater use of partnerships with the private sector, particularly banks. Banks could work with insurers and reinsurers to maintain trade credit and contain the rapidly rising cost of maritime insurance.
That could reduce the pressure on governments to continually draw on sovereign funds or seek additional external financing. But there is a limit to how long these measures can compensate for a fundamental disruption to trade.
If the war and interruption to shipping continue into 2027, Darwish says Gulf states could face a genuine challenge in meeting financial obligations and preserving monetary stability.
Kareem Ramadan is a Muscat-based correspondent for The New Arab's Arabic edition, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defense forces down 71 Russian drones overnight
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defense forces down 71 Russian drones overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook.
Starting at 18:00 on Sunday, September 6, Russian forces launched 92 combat drones, including jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera drones, Parodiya decoy drones, and S8000 Banderol drones, from the directions of Oryol, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, temporarily occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by Ukrainian aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:00 on Monday, September 7, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 71 drones.
Hits were recorded at 12 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at one location.
As reported by Ukrinform, four people were injured in a Russian strike on Sloviansk in the evening of September 6.

articles.title: Sochi oil depot reportedly erupts in flames again days after Ukrainian strikes
articles.body:
An oil depot in the Russian city of Sochi appeared to reignite on Sept. 7, three days after being struck by Ukrainian drones, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Videos posted by Sochi residents on social media appear to show the oil depot, owned by Russia's state energy company Rosneft, ablaze and billowing smoke. The Russian monitoring Telegram channel ExileNova+ reports that authorities are asking local residents to close their windows due to heavy smoke in the coastal vacation destination.
At the time of publishing the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports nor the extent of the damage caused.
It was not immediately clear as to what caused the oil depot to reportedly reignite. Russian Air raid alerts in the region were not activated ahead of the blaze.
The latest fires come days after Ukrainian forces launched several waves of attacks against targets in Sochi on Sept. 3-4, including a naval drone strike on a Russian vessel.
Known as Russia’s "Second Capital," Sochi is home to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s official summer residence. Considered a winter playground for Russia’s elite, the city is located approximately 650 to 700 kilometers (400 to 435 miles) from the Ukraine border.
For months, Ukraine has conducted a sustained campaign of drone and missile strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. Damage to energy facilities has prompted Moscow to impose export restrictions as domestic supplies have tightened and long queues have formed across the country.
Ukraine's General Staff announced on September 4 that two major Russian oil facilities have suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes in August. 
Lukoil's NORSI refinery in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, located about 800 kilometers (nearly 500 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was shut down due to damage suffered in a Ukrainian drone attack on Aug. 26. The facility is Russia's fourth-largest oil refinery and second-largest gasoline producer, processing around 15-17 million metric tons of crude oil annually. 
The General Staff also said the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex in Slobidka, Leningrad Oblast, had suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes on Sept. 1. Located about 850 kilometers (nearly 530 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the facility is one of Russia's largest ports on the Baltic Sea and home to an oil terminal that serves as a major hub for exporting crude oil and petroleum products.

articles.title: Witkoff and Kushner likely brought substantive proposal to Moscow – experts to RT (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Witkoff and Kushner likely brought substantive proposal to Moscow – experts to RT (VIDEO)
There are grounds for cautious optimism following Saturday’s talks between US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl and ex-White House aide Steve Gill have told RT.
Trump’s son-in-law and the US special envoy likely presented concrete and well-developed ideas on ending the Ukraine conflict to the Russian leadership, Kneissl and Gill surmised.
According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, the talks, which lasted over three hours and included formal discussions as well as an informal exchange over lunch, were “substantive, constructive, extremely candid and trusting.” Aside from the Ukraine conflict, the two sides are understood to have discussed economic cooperation and potential “major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects.”
Witkoff and Kushner subsequently departed for Kiev, where they were slated to hold meetings with Vladimir Zelensky and other Ukrainian officials.
Speaking to RT on Sunday, former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl said that “there is apparently something materializing because these two persons would not come without anything in their hands.” She also claimed that “trust is there” between Moscow and Washington, citing “this ongoing direct communication on a high-ranking political level.”
Kneissl also pointed to the previously unannounced visit to the Russian capital by CIA Director John Ratcliffe last Tuesday, during which he met with Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) chief Sergei Naryshkin.
On Sunday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov likewise said that Saturday’s negotiations were indicative of an “atmosphere of trust” between Russia and the US.
Conservative media host Steve Gill, who served in the office of the US Trade Representative under Presidents George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton, concurred with Kneissl, saying that he was “optimistic that the meeting took as long as it did.”
He told RT that the trip Witkoff and Kushner made to Moscow was likely preceded by considerable preparatory work, with Trump’s envoys plausibly bringing a substantive proposal to the Russian capital.
“The fact that it took three hours to kind of work through those details and now they’re heading to Ukraine leaves me at least optimistic that hopefully some progress was made today,” Gill concluded.

articles.title: North Korea vows nuclear-armed navy as US ally drills open
articles.body:
This picture taken on September 6, 2026 and released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on September 7, 2026 shows North Korean leader Kim Jong Un touring the destroyer "Kang Kon" during a commissioning ceremony for the destroyer at Wonsan Port in Kangwon Province. (AFP Photo/KCNA via KNS)
Leader Kim Jong Un vowed to build North Korea’s navy into a nuclear-armed force, state media reported on Sept. 7 as U.S. allies’ maritime drills kicked off.
This week’s maneuvers involving Japan, South Korea and the United States were established in 2023 in what officials called an effort to deter Pyongyang’s missile and nuclear threats.
Kim’s comments came at the commissioning of the Kang Kon, a warship that partially capsized when launched in May 2025, in the port city of Wonsan on Sept. 6, the official Korean Central News Agency reported.
“We should make sure that the diversified and effective operation of nuclear combat systems is conducted for an actual war through developing our navy into a nuclear armed force,” Kim reportedly told the ceremony.
“Once ordered anytime, the new-generation destroyer should deal a deadly retaliatory blow at the enemies as it is a force involved in the state nuclear counteraction system,” he said.
Photos released of Kim showed him accompanied by his daughter, Ju Ae, who is reportedly designated as a successor to her father.
Kim oversaw in July a test of the Kang Kon, one of two 5,000-ton class warships launched last year, just over a year after it was damaged during its launch.

articles.title: Yemeni army reports 13 airstrikes on Houthi positions
articles.body:
Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Yemeni warplanes carried out 13 airstrikes early Monday on positions, gatherings and military vehicles of the Houthi group in central Yemen, including a missile launcher, the army said.
The strikes targeted sites in the Al-Sharyah, Dhi Na’im, Al-Bayda and Al-Sawadiyah districts of Al-Bayda governorate, according to the Yemeni Armed Forces Media Center.
In a separate operation in southern Al-Dhale governorate, warplanes destroyed a Houthi command-and-control room and a thermal surveillance system on Mount Nasa in the Murais front, the military said.
The aircraft also struck Houthi gatherings in the area.
Hours earlier, the Yemeni army said it had retaken positions in Taiz and Al-Hudaydah governorates during clashes that left more than 20 Houthi fighters killed or wounded.
The military also reported airstrikes on Houthi positions in Taiz, Al-Hudaydah, Marib and Al-Jawf governorates.
Several fronts across Yemen have recently witnessed renewed fighting amid an escalation in reciprocal attacks since July, ending a period of relative calm that had largely prevailed since a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.

articles.title: Ukraine has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones en masse, Zelenskyy says. Only three to five have real results
articles.body:
Ukraine now has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones en masse, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He gave the number at a Kyiv press conference alongside US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ukrinform reported.
Most of those firms are still chasing the problem, and only a few have working systems. The race matters because Russia's jet-powered Geran drones fly too fast for the mobile gun teams that once downed the slower models. Russia has sharply expanded the jets' use over the summer, launching them by day as well as by night and driving air-raid alerts over Kyiv almost hourly.
Prototypes outnumber proven interceptors
"Today, we have about 60 companies in Ukraine already working on intercepting jet-powered drones, and doing so on a mass scale. To be precise, there are 67," Zelenskyy said.
He added that three to five have shown real results, and the next step is mass production.
Zelenskyy calls it all "Plan B"
Zelenskyy framed the entire defensive build-up as a fallback.
"All this defense is 'Plan B,' though right now it is very relevant. 'Plan A' is to accelerate diplomatic possibilities as much as possible, to reduce escalation from Russia," he said.
He spoke as the US envoys pressed a peace push in Kyiv, with no breakthrough announced.
He also called anti-ballistic defense Ukraine's weak point, saying he would raise it in upcoming meetings in Norway and Canada, and that the US plans to increase production of Patriot interceptors next year while Germany expands its own output under existing licenses.
Ukraine needs the interceptors to down Russian ballistic missiles that come several times per week. Each Russian attack on Kyiv costs the city budget about $12 million. More than four thousand buildings in Kyiv have been damaged by Russian strikes, with each attack adding to a repair bill the city carries alongside the human losses.

articles.title: Iran to declare new ‘restricted zone’ outside Strait of Hormuz – official
articles.body:
Iran to declare new ‘restricted zone’ outside Strait of Hormuz – official
Iran will announce a new “restricted zone” for shipping outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days, high-ranking security official Mohsen Rezaei has said.
The US resumed strikes on Iranian targets last week, saying they were in response to Tehran hitting commercial ships in the key waterway. The Islamic Republic maintains that no vessel can pass through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for the shipment of some 20% of global oil, without its permission. Iran retaliated with a missile and drone barrage against US military facilities in the Gulf, while also firing at American warships, including an aircraft carrier.
In a televised interview on Sunday, Rezaei, who is the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran plans to place even wider curbs on shipping in the region.
The restricted area “will begin from the US Navy’s blockade line and extend into parts of the Persian Gulf,” stretching toward several key ports, he said.
“Any vessel entering this new zone will be placed on a sanctions list,” which will have consequences for its insurance and future passage through the strait, the security official explained.
Rezaei insisted that the Strait of Hormuz remains “completely closed and under the control of the armed forces” of Iran, describing US President Donald Trump’s claims that it’s open as a “big lie.”
More than a hundred vessels passed through the waterway on a daily basis before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in late February, but now the number has reduced to only seven or eight per day, the official said. Those vessels are transporting essential goods for the Islamic Republic, he added.
“The Americans are trying to smuggle five to six vessels through at great expense, but these ships are usually struck,” Rezaei stressed.
Iran isn’t sinking those ships because they are carrying oil and doing so would harm the environment, he stressed.
On Saturday, the US attacked three Iranian commercial vessels as part of its blockade of Tehran’s ports, with one of them, the crude oil tanker M/T Kylo, sinking in the Gulf of Oman the next day.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth warned in a post on X that Washington could target the Iranian oil tanker fleet in the Middle East or in the Indo-Pacific region. “It’s simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers,” he wrote.
Iranian Parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned on Sunday that further aggressive actions by the US will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” retaliation by Tehran.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases was only a start,” Ghalibaf said.

articles.title: Ukraine's intelligence chief responds to alleged "war between Ukrainian special services"
articles.body:
Ukraine's intelligence chief responds to alleged "war between Ukrainian special services"
Oleh Ivashchenko, Head of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), has commented on the confrontation between the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and DIU, stating that an isolated incident should not be generalised and projected onto entire institutions.
Source: Ivashchenko's interview with Ukrinform
Quote: "There are no grounds to extrapolate an isolated incident onto state institutions and security services in particular. In our work, secrecy is closely linked to oversight, and operational freedom always operates within the framework of state interests."
Details: The head of military intelligence made these comments when asked about the recent confrontation between the DIU and SSU in the Dniprovskyi district of Kyiv and why an incident involving specific individuals was quickly described as a "war between special services".
Ivashchenko also noted that "both Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Security Service of Ukraine, although they have different functions, work against a common enemy in the interests of national security".
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps said that its deputy commander for combat operations, Stepan Kaplunov, had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of the building where he was living.
- On the morning of 2 September, reports spread on social media about a shootout said to be between Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Security Service of Ukraine in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance.
- Meanwhile, the SSU said in the morning that, together with DIU, it had foiled a terrorist attack against a leader of a Russian opposition political national movement who had arrived in Ukraine.
- Later, Kaplunov's lawyer, Taras Borovskyi, said that the serviceman had been released, but his whereabouts were unknown.
- On the morning of 3 September, the SSU released a video in which Kaplunov admitted to having links to Russia's Federal Security Service and said an attempt had been made to recruit him to assassinate Ukrainian military personnel and other individuals. However, his lawyer insists that the confession was made under duress.
- On 3 September, Kaplunov himself also stated that he had been abducted by SSU officers and described his time in a "secret prison", where he was threatened with "disappearing forever".
- Kaplunov also said that the SSU had attempted, with his help, to discredit Dmytro Ivanov, deputy commander of the Timur Special Unit, and Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the President's Office.
- Officers from the State Bureau of Investigation have opened a pre-trial investigation into the circumstances of the confrontation between SSU officers and DIU servicemen.
- On 3 September, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine said that a disinformation campaign aimed at discrediting the military intelligence agency and its units has been launched, with media outlets, bloggers and Telegram channels expected to be involved.

articles.title: Iran to declare ‘prohibited zone’ near Hormuz Strait in coming day
articles.body:
Iran will declare a new “restricted” maritime zone outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days, the country’s top national security official has said, warning that any vessel entering the area would be placed on a sanctions list.
In a televised interview late on Sept. 6, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said the zone will begin from the U.S. Navy’s blockade line and extend into parts of the Gulf, according to the Iranian state-run Press TV.
“Any vessel entering this new zone will be placed on a sanctions list,” he said.
Rezaei also said Iran and Oman would sign an agreement in the coming days on the new corridor through Hormuz, with its entry and exit points under Iranian control.
He said the Strait of Hormuz was “completely closed and under the control of the armed forces,” dismissing U.S. President Donald Trump’s claim that the strategic waterway remained open as a “big lie.”
Before Iran closed the strait, more than 100 ships carrying over 100 million tons of cargo passed through it daily, Rezaei said. He added that only seven or eight ships carrying essential goods for Iran were now transiting the waterway.
“The Americans are trying to smuggle five to six vessels through at great expense, but these ships are usually struck,” he said, without elaborating.
Rezaei said Iran had decided against sinking the vessels because they were carrying oil and doing so would damage the region’s environment.
He also claimed that Iran had successfully tested a new anti-ship missile above a US Navy vessel 48 hours earlier.
“For the first time, we tested our anti-ship missile above an American warship,” he said.
“This special missile created hell for the Americans, and they fled,” he added, without identifying the vessel or specifying where the test occurred.
He separately rejected claims that the US economic blockade was causing widespread famine in Iran.
“The claim that the U.S. economic blockade is causing a major famine in Iran is a big lie,” Rezaei told Iranian state broadcaster IRIB.
“The Iranian government has been preparing for this for a long time and has sufficient stocks of food and essential goods,” he added.
Meanwhile, the Iranian Foreign Ministry on Sept. 7 warned South Korea against military deployment or involvement in U.S. operations in the Strait of Hormuz, saying such a move would have “serious consequences.”
On Sept. 4, Seoul said it was considering “contributions” to U.S. security efforts in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has largely controlled since the outbreak of war against the United States on Feb. 28.

articles.title: China Updates Defense Mobilization Law to Enable Rapid Transition to Martial Law
articles.body:
China has revised its national defense mobilization law, allowing Beijing to transition the country from peacetime to wartime more quickly in the event of a serious threat.
The Ministry of National Defense of the People’s Republic of China announced this.
The law will take effect on October 1, 2026.
The Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress approved the amendments on August 28. The document sets out procedures for mobilizing military and civilian resources in the event of a threat to China’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security.
The new rules may primarily apply to a potential conflict over Taiwan. At the same time, they could also be invoked in the event of a war with other countries with which China has territorial disputes, including the Philippines, India, and Japan.
China already has a law allowing the use of “non-peaceful means” against supporters of Taiwan independence. The new rules supplement this legal framework with mechanisms for mobilizing the country’s resources.
One of the main changes concerns civilian resources. The new law allows the state not only to requisition property but also to expropriate it.
In the event of mobilization, the authorities will be able to set priorities for the financial system, transportation, information networks, energy, and water supply. These resources may be directed toward the needs of China’s People’s Liberation Army.
The new rules may also allow the state to mobilize resources from government institutions, companies, organizations, and private individuals during wartime call to arms.
In early July 2026, Militarnyi reported that President of China Xi Jinping outlined a vision for China’s future that calls for strengthening the country’s military capabilities, expanding its international influence, and shaping a new global order.
Military power was one of the central themes of his speech. The Chinese leader linked the country’s future to the continued development of its armed forces.
According to Xi Jinping, China should strengthen political control over the military, pursue military reforms, develop defense technologies, strengthen personnel capabilities, and improve its military management system.

news
U.S. pushes to revive Ukraine–Russia talks after Witkoff and Kushner meet Zelensky in Kyiv
Source: Suspilne
- Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine’s leadership held three rounds of talks in Kyiv with an official U.S. delegation led by Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The meetings focused on ending the war, support through the winter and security guarantees. Representatives from France, Britain and Germany joined the talks later.
- The sides acknowledged that the war will most likely continue until winter. Zelensky said Ukraine hopes to reach an agreement with U.S. partners and receive support from European allies “if the war continues into the winter, which for now appears likely.” Trump’s envoys told Zelensky and his team that progress could still be made before winter, according to sources who spoke to the Financial Times.
- The United States wants to resume trilateral talks with Russia and Ukraine, last held about six months ago. Witkoff said he hoped a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States would be announced “in the near future.” “I think we made significant progress in Moscow. We heard new ideas,” he said. Kushner said Trump had tasked him and Witkoff with creating a “peace package” and was focused on “how to create a framework that will actually build a durable peace.”
- Ukraine has strengthened its position on the battlefield, giving it greater confidence regardless of how future talks are structured, Zelensky said. He added that every effort should be made to ensure trilateral meetings take place. “We’ll see what Russia agrees to.”
- Trump’s envoys brought “updated versions” of earlier documents to Kyiv, revised “to reflect the changed circumstances,” according to sources who spoke to the Financial Times. The sources said, however, that the envoys had brought few new ideas and that control of the Donbas remained the central issue. Zelensky also said it was one of the key issues in peace talks. “This is not just about the Donbas. I think it is about the war as a whole,” he said.
- Witkoff called the trip wonderful and said the U.S. delegation was very satisfied with the results of the talks in Kyiv and Moscow. Zelensky said Witkoff and Kushner’s visit to Ukraine was “important and productive.” Today, you were even more effective than the Patriot air defense systems protecting our people here in the capital,” he said. “Come more often, and we’ll have a chance to live a little.”

articles.title: Ukraine eliminates suspected killer of military intelligence General Shapoval in occupied Donetsk – media

Ukraine eliminates suspected killer of military intelligence General Shapoval in occupied Donetsk – media
Sources in the Ukrainian intelligence services told LB.ua, according to Ukrinform. They also provided photographs that they said showed surveillance of Shutov and his elimination.
According to the publication’s sources, the operation was carried out by Ukrainian intelligence services in the occupied territory. Shutov was reportedly killed after an improvised explosive device was planted in his Subaru and detonated when he arrived at the Dynamo sports complex in Donetsk’s Leninskyi district in the evening of July 27.
Local occupation-affiliated information resources reported the incident as a “nighttime UAV attack that injured the head of the sports wrestling federation.” However, according to LB.ua’s sources, Shutov was killed in a car explosion.
According to the sources, information about Shutov’s elimination was not released immediately after the operation for security reasons, until the intelligence and combat group had returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Oleh Shutov was president of the so-called DPR Judo and Sambo Association and an operational officer with the special operations center of the so-called DPR Ministry of State Security, which was controlled by Russian intelligence services. In April 2024, Russian occupation authorities abolished the so-called DPR Ministry of State Security and transferred its functions to the local FSB directorate.
Then-SSU chief Vasyl Hrytsak was the first to publicly identify Shutov’s involvement on April 19, 2019. “Shutov Oleg Nikolaevich, born March 9, 1966, a resident of Donetsk. It was this individual who planted an explosive device under the car of Ukrainian military intelligence general Maksym Shapoval on June 26, 2017. Today, for the first time, we are making public information about the perpetrator of this terrorist attack,” Hrytsak said at the time.
According to Hrytsak, Shutov had rented an apartment in the building where Shapoval lived, as well as a parking space near the location where the general parked his car.
On June 27, 2017, Maksym Shapoval was killed when a car bomb exploded in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district.
According to Hrytsak, about an hour after carrying out the attack, Shutov packed his belongings from the rented apartment and left Kyiv, traveling to Russia and then to Donbas.
Shutov was also implicated in the bombing of the car of SSU Colonel Oleksandr Kharaberiush in Mariupol on March 31, 2017.
According to the SSU, the organizers of both killings of Ukrainian officers were Russian FSB Lieutenant General Dmitry Minayev, head of the FSB department for counterintelligence operations, and his subordinate, Vasily Yevdokimov, head of the so-called DPR Ministry of State Security special operations center, known by the nickname Lenin.
In April 2019, the SSU announced the detention of seven members of a Russian sabotage and reconnaissance group, two of whom were career officers of the Russian intelligence services. SSU operatives also established a connection between the group and Oleg Shutov. The group had planned to assassinate a military intelligence officer; one of the saboteurs was killed when an explosive device detonated while it was being planted under the officer’s car.

articles.title: Germany to Create Comprehensive Measures to Counter Russian Sabotage and Cyberattacks
articles.body:
Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior plans to establish a comprehensive set of measures to counter Russian sabotage, including cyberattacks.
Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told this to Bild.
The security plan calls for the rapid deployment of special units in strategically important cities across the country — Berlin, Munich, Hamburg, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt, Leipzig, Hanover and Cologne.
They are to provide comprehensive protection against drones in the airspace over critical infrastructure, airports, railway stations and the government district of the capital. In addition to interception, their duties will also include neutralizing explosive devices.
“Hybrid attacks involving drones carrying explosives targeting airports, agents in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks and sabotage of our infrastructure — this is our daily reality. These attacks will intensify, but we can defend ourselves,” the minister said.
Under the security plan, drone protection in the near future will be provided not only by the federal police but also by critical infrastructure operators, including energy companies and defense contractors. They will be given legal authority to actively repel drone attacks.
In addition, Germany also plans to create a national protective shield, known as the Cyberdome.
According to the minister, the network is to detect and block attempts by hackers to launch attacks at an early stage.
The security plan is being developed amid Russian hybrid threats. On August 5, a drone equipped with explosives was found near a Ukrainian An-124 Ruslan transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport during the night. Militarnyi reported on the incident.
On September 1, Germany officially accused Russia of the attack involving the Ukrainian An-124 in Leipzig.
On September 2, German law enforcement authorities confirmed that a Russian-born man with a Latvian passport and a Belarusian citizen who also holds a Russian passport were involved in the planned attack.
On September 3, amid Russia’s attempted sabotage in Leipzig, Germany strengthened cooperation with Ukraine and drafted a plan to expand its military contingent in Lithuania.

articles.title: ‘Mayday’ film review: Kenneth Branagh plays ‘a good Russian’ for a change as a former KGB officer who loves Top Gun and fights like Liam Neeson
articles.body:
‘Mayday’ film review: Kenneth Branagh plays ‘a good Russian’ for a change as a former KGB officer who loves Top Gun and fights like Liam Neeson
A film about a downed U.S. Navy pilot and a former KGB officer who become friends while trying to escape the Soviet Union in 1987 is now streaming on Apple TV. Shakespearean actor Kenneth Branagh once again plays a Soviet citizen — hardly new territory in his career — while Ryan Reynolds sticks to his familiar persona. The film was commissioned by Skydance Media, a studio that reportedly has close ties to the Trump administration. Critic Eduard Zhuravlev examines what a campy, cliché-ridden Hollywood portrayal of the Soviet Union can look like in 2026.
It’s 1987. Dashing U.S. Navy pilot Troy Kelly (Canadian actor Ryan Reynolds) accepts a secret CIA mission: fly a reconnaissance plane into the Arkhangelsk region to find out whether the Soviet leadership is building missile silos there. The mission goes wrong. Kelly’s plane is hit, and he is forced to eject over the snow-covered taiga. In the forest, the wounded American is rescued by bearded carpenter Nikolai Ustinov (Irish actor Kenneth Branagh), a former KGB officer who is anti-Soviet and a huge fan of the action movie Top Gun. Ustinov agrees to help Kelly escape; a ruthless “Red Army” led by “head of internal security” Alexander Volkov (Polish actor Marcin Dorocinski) is already hunting him.
Mayday may seem like just another streaming action movie destined to fade from memory before the credits finish rolling. These movies usually star some Chris — Evans (The Gray Man, Ghosted), Pratt (Mercy, The Tomorrow War), or Hemsworth (Extraction, Extraction 2). This time, though, viewers got lucky — and not because the lead happens to be a Ryan. Reynolds has plenty of streaming junk on his own résumé.
Mayday is a funny, propulsive buddy road comedy that holds its own even against 1980s genre classics. It also reimagines the caricatured Soviet clichés Hollywood produced in abundance during the Reagan era, from Red Dawn and Rocky IV to Red Heat and Rambo III. That makes it a politically charged film.
John Francis Daley and Jonathan Goldstein wrote and directed the film. Their credits include the reboot of the 1980s comedy series Vacation, the hilarious and hard-edged comedy Game Night, the brisk fantasy Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, and the screenplays for Horrible Bosses and Spider-Man: Homecoming. The pair could easily rank among Hollywood’s most skilled comedy filmmakers working today.
Skydance Media is another important “author” here — the same studio that merged with Paramount, plans to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, and reportedly has close ties to the Trump administration. Its résumé includes not only the Terminator and Mission: Impossible sequels and a good half of the mass-market schlock starring the Chrises mentioned above, but also films about the complicated relationship between East and West, including The Gorge and Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit.
Branagh, incidentally, directed Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit and played its main villain, Russian oligarch Viktor Cherevin, who plots a terrorist attack on Wall Street. Branagh, an award-winning filmmaker known for adaptations of Shakespeare and Agatha Christie — plus one Marvel outing — has played a Russian character roughly once every six years. After Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit came Tenet, in which the Irish actor played another Russian oligarch, Andrei Sator. International relations are almost beside the point for Sator: dying and bent on revenge, he is prepared to destroy the world. Now Branagh has unexpectedly played “a good Russian.” True, Ustinov is a former KGB officer who tortured people on the job, but the filmmakers show little interest in that detail.
This is one of the first roles in Branagh’s career that has asked him to throw punches. The 65-year-old Irishman does a remarkably convincing Liam Neeson impression in action scenes, at times staged with the choreographic swagger of Atomic Blonde and the John Wick films. In one scene, filmed almost entirely without cuts, the unflappable comrade takes out a group of volunteer patrolmen with a pool rack to the tune of Belaya cheremukha; in another, he dispatches an entire train car full of Red Army soldiers — literally.
Branagh’s unexpected performance — his character recalls Robin Williams’s Soviet saxophonist in Moscow on the Hudson — easily overshadows Reynolds’s efforts. Troy Kelly is yet another exhausting, chatty wisecracker in Reynolds’s career; the actor has not dropped the persona even off camera in roughly 15 years. Still, the two actors have chemistry to rival Deadpool and Wolverine.
The filmmakers bring plenty of wit of their own. For starters, Mayday is both the international distress signal Kelly transmits and simply “a day in May” — the final showdown unfolds on Red Square in the middle of the Victory Day parade.
Moscow was filmed in Budapest, as usual, but with respect and humor. Ustinov drinks moonshine and eats bear meat, but the clichés are played for laughs rather than treated seriously. The actors playing Russian characters either speak Russian without a foreign accent or clearly make an effort. A Party apparatchik keeps The Atheist’s Dictionary and The Luzhin Defense at his dacha; a village grandmother keeps a jar of chicory on a shelf. There is even a Wes Anderson-style montage of a ride in a Zhiguli past Stalinist skyscrapers, Khrushchev-era apartment blocks, and a combined heat and power plant — all set to Bruce Springsteen.
Volkov, a revanchist played with impish gusto by Polish actor Marcin Dorocinski — who also played chess player Vasily Borgov in The Queen’s Gambit and the unnamed captain of the sunken submarine Sevastopol in the latest Mission: Impossible films — keeps a portrait of Chernenko in his office. Before you have time to think the filmmakers are off by two years, Chernenko is replaced by Gorbachev. “I didn’t want to hang a portrait of the man who’s destroying my country,” Volkov says. He dreams of restoring the empire and putting an end to glasnost.
At the same time, the filmmakers urge people to get along, discard propaganda slogans, and stop equating “Party policy” with individual citizens. At first, Kelly says, “Silence is complicity,” and calls everyone living in the Soviet Union part of the problem. He gradually changes his mind both about supposedly faceless Soviet people and about American democracy, after learning that his father developed cancer from asbestos exposure. Ustinov also revises his view of America, which had been shaped by the militaristic propaganda in Top Gun.
The filmmakers’ love for the biggest hit of 1986 is, of course, another meta-joke. It is hard to imagine a KGB officer born in the 1920s — even a former one — watching a bootleg VHS tape of an action movie about young, muscular pilots facing unidentified MiGs 100 times a year. The joke seems intended to remind us that ideological manifestos can be found in pop culture, not just in scientific communism classes.
Skydance Media also made Top Gun: Maverick, the sequel released 36 years after the original — and the highest-grossing film of Tom Cruise’s career. In 1986, Ustinov had to watch the movie on a bootleg VHS tape (“You could go to prison for that!”); by 2022, Maverick was playing in theaters near Arkhangelsk through gray-market distribution. The franchise makes a fitting symbol: a book about the brief period without a Cold War could well be titled “From Top Gun to Top Gun.”

US Envoys Say Putin Talks Were “Very Constructive,” Sees Opening for Trilateral Format
US President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, outlining a pathway toward renewed peace talks and expressing hope for a trilateral format soon.
The two envoys outlined their assessment during remarks in Kyiv, a day after meeting the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, in Moscow, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent on September 6.
Kushner told reporters that Washington had consulted both sides about reviving three-way negotiations. "One thing Steve and I really thought would be productive is to go back to the trilateral format," he explained. "We've spoken with both parties, and so hopefully we'll have progress on that very soon."
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Witkoff stated that Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had dispatched the pair to reopen talks. "The President asked Jared and me to come here and to restart conversations, negotiations, because this is so important to him," he noted.
Kushner characterized the Moscow talks as constructive and substantive, with both delegations posing questions about the elements of a durable settlement.
Witkoff, who has made about eight visits to the Russian capital to meet Putin, emphasized the role of personal ties in ending the war. He and Kushner have traveled there together at least three times. "Relationships are critical in terms of solving conflicts like this," Witkoff declared.
The envoys met Putin first to gauge Moscow's position and briefed Zelenskyy's team on the discussion. Witkoff stated that their task is to bring the two sides together, narrow the issues between them, and build reliable communication channels.
He described the previous 48 hours as a constructive start and expressed confidence in an eventual resolution.
The Kyiv visit was the envoys' first trip to the Ukrainian capital, which they reached by train after their aircraft landed in Poland. Ukraine had readied its airports to receive the delegation by air, but Russian strikes ruled out a direct landing.
At the railway station, they were met by senior Ukrainian officials, including presidential office chief Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy Serhii Kyslytsia, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia.
The timing carries added weight as winter nears, with Moscow calculating that Ukrainian resolve will weaken through the cold months and that Putin's willingness to negotiate will fade until the season ends in mid-March.
The Kyiv talks followed directly from a marathon session in Moscow the previous day. There, Witkoff and Kushner spent more than three hours with Putin—three hours and 10 minutes in all—focused primarily on approaches to ending the war in Ukraine.
Officials on both sides framed the exchange as substantive and unusually frank, and the delegation was reported to have arrived with a range of settlement proposals. The discussions extended beyond Ukraine to potential large-scale US-Russian economic projects.
The Moscow visit unfolded under a temporary arrangement on strikes. Putin had ordered Russian forces to refrain from hitting Kyiv for three days from midnight on September 5, and Zelenskyy signaled Ukraine's readiness to observe a matching halt on cities tied to the negotiations.
